Design with Azure RBAC, soft delete and purge protection, private endpoints, rotation policies, and managed identities so apps never hold credentials.
lessons.deep:
**Choosing the service**
- **Key Vault Standard**: software-protected keys, secrets, certificates.
- **Key Vault Premium**: adds HSM-backed keys in a multitenant service.
- **Managed HSM**: dedicated, **single-tenant** HSM pools with their own **security domain**, **local RBAC** that subscription owners can't override, FIPS 140-3 Level 3. Choose it for strict key-custody requirements or high-throughput CMK.

**Design rules**
- **One vault per application per environment per region** to limit blast radius.
- **Azure RBAC** for data-plane access (now the default model): Key Vault Secrets User for apps, Key Vault Crypto Officer for key admins, Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User for services doing wrap/unwrap (CMK).
- **Soft delete** is always on (7–90 days, default 90). Enable **purge protection** (can't be turned off once on) — required for many CMK scenarios.
- Network: disable public access, use **private endpoints**.
- **Rotation**: key rotation policies; certificate auto-renewal with integrated CAs (DigiCert, GlobalSign); **Event Grid** near-expiry events to trigger automation.
- Apps authenticate with **managed identities**.
- Log to Log Analytics via diagnostic settings; Defender for Key Vault detects unusual access.
- Find hard-coded secrets in code with **GitHub Advanced Security** secret scanning.

terms.d: Single-tenant, customer-controlled HSM pool with local RBAC and its own security domain.
Prevents permanent deletion of a soft-deleted vault/object until retention expires.
Encrypted blob of Managed HSM's root keys, held by the customer for recovery.
Key Vault setting that rotates key versions automatically on a schedule.

lessons.trap: Vault access policies are legacy; Azure RBAC is the recommended model. And soft delete alone doesn't stop a malicious admin purging keys — purge protection does.
lessons.example: A payments team stores its CMK in Managed HSM so cloud subscription owners can't grant themselves key access, and enables purge protection to satisfy the storage CMK requirement.

lessons.title: Enterprise access model for privileged roles
lessons.short: The enterprise access model replaces the old AD tier model with a control plane, a management plane and a data/workload plane, plus user and app access pathways. Privileged roles are assigned and delegated so lower planes can never control higher ones.
lessons.deep:
Microsoft's **enterprise access model** evolves the AD **Tier 0/1/2** model for hybrid and multicloud:
- **Control plane** (expanded Tier 0): identity and access control for the whole enterprise: Entra ID Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator, AD DS domain controllers, Entra Connect, AD FS, AD CS, PIM, Conditional Access, and network access control where it's the only control (OT).
- **Management plane** (part of Tier 1): enterprise-wide IT management, such as subscription owners and Intune admins.
- **Data/workload plane** (part of Tier 1): per-workload and per-app administration, often by DevOps teams.
- **User access** and **app access** (former Tier 2): employees, partners, customers and APIs.

**Design principles for role assignment and delegation**
- Lower planes must never control higher planes (no Tier 1 admin can reset a Tier 0 password or edit a Tier 0 GPO).
- **Least privilege**: built-in roles with the smallest scope, such as User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator, or **administrative units** to scope by region, instead of Global Administrator.
- **Just-in-time** elevation with PIM; few permanent assignments.
- Separate admin accounts (cloud-only for Entra privileged roles), used only from **PAWs**.
- Azure: assign at management group/subscription only when needed; delegate resource-group scope to workload teams.
- Keep two or more **emergency access** accounts.

terms.d: Enterprise access model plane holding identity and access control systems (expanded Tier 0).
Plane for enterprise-wide IT management functions.
Entra container that scopes directory role assignments to a subset of users, groups or devices.
Break-glass cloud-only Global Administrator account for lockout recovery.

lessons.trap: Entra Connect servers, AD CS and PIM belong to the control plane (Tier 0), not the management plane; treating them as ordinary servers is the common error.
lessons.example: A regional helpdesk gets Helpdesk Administrator scoped to an 'EMEA users' administrative unit instead of User Administrator tenant-wide.

lessons.title: Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management gives just-in-time, time-bound, approval-based activation of Entra roles, Azure resource roles and group membership (PIM for Groups). Eligible assignments are activated on demand with MFA or authentication context, justification and approval.
lessons.deep:
**PIM** (Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance) removes standing privilege.

**Assignment types**
- **Eligible**: user must activate before using the role.
- **Active**: role is usable immediately (keep for emergency access only).
- Both can be permanent or time-bound (start/end dates).

**Role settings (per role)**
- **Activation maximum duration**: 1–24 hours.
- On activation require **MFA** or a **Conditional Access authentication context** (for example, phishing-resistant MFA from a PAW).
- Require **justification**, **ticket information** (not validated) and **approval** (choose explicit approvers).
- Notifications and alerts (for example, roles assigned outside PIM).

**Scope**
- Microsoft Entra roles, **Azure resource roles** (management group to resource), and **PIM for Groups** (just-in-time membership or ownership of a security group, which can carry app access or role-assignable roles).

**Audit and review**
- PIM audit history and **access reviews** of role assignments.
- Requires Privileged Role Administrator to configure Entra role settings.

PIM controls *activation*; protect the *use* of a role with a CA policy scoped to directory roles or protected actions.

terms.d: PIM assignment that must be activated before the role can be used.
Just-in-time membership or ownership of security groups.
How long an activation lasts, 1 to 24 hours.
PIM setting requiring a named approver before activation succeeds.

lessons.trap: PIM's MFA-on-activation doesn't protect a role after activation or for permanent active assignments; the fix combines eligible assignments with CA or protected actions.
lessons.example: Exchange Administrators are eligible for up to 4 hours, must satisfy authentication context c2 (phishing-resistant MFA on a compliant device) and need approval from the messaging lead.

lessons.title: Entitlement management and Entra ID Governance
lessons.short: Entitlement management bundles groups, apps, SharePoint sites and roles into access packages with request, approval, expiry and review policies, including for external users from connected organizations. Microsoft Entra ID Governance adds lifecycle workflows and advanced features beyond Entra ID P2.
lessons.deep:
**Entitlement management** (identity governance) automates access request workflows.
- **Catalog**: a container of resources and access packages, delegated to catalog owners.
- **Access package**: groups/teams, applications, SharePoint sites (and in preview, Entra roles) assigned together.
- **Policies**: who can request (internal users, specific **connected organizations**, any external user), approval stages, requestor questions, **expiration**, **separation of duties** (incompatible packages) and recurring **access reviews**.
- External users get a B2B guest account on approval; when their last assignment expires, the guest can be blocked and removed automatically.

**Licensing**
- **Entra ID P2**: PIM, access reviews (core), entitlement management (basic).
- **Microsoft Entra ID Governance** (requires P1 or P2): **lifecycle workflows** (joiner/mover/leaver), custom extensions (Logic Apps), **Verified ID** in access packages, auto-assignment policies, machine-learning-assisted access reviews, inactive-user reviews, PIM for Groups reviews, and integration with ID Protection and Purview Insider Risk Management.
- New IGA features are released in ID Governance, not P2.

**Lifecycle workflows** automate tasks such as generating a Temporary Access Pass before day one, or removing groups and licences at departure.

terms.d: Bundle of resource roles requested and assigned together with a policy.
External directory or domain whose users may request access packages.
ID Governance automation for joiner, mover and leaver tasks.
Access package check that blocks incompatible combinations.

lessons.trap: Lifecycle workflows and Verified ID requirements in access packages need Entra ID Governance, not just P2.
lessons.example: A supplier is added as a connected organization; its staff request a 'Supplier portal' package approved by a sponsor, expiring after 90 days with a quarterly review.

lessons.title: AD DS security, governance and attack resilience
lessons.short: Evaluate AD DS against common attacks: pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, Kerberoasting, DCSync, Golden Ticket and AD CS abuse. Resilience comes from tiering, credential hygiene, Defender for Identity detections, lateral movement path reviews and a tested forest recovery plan.
lessons.deep:
**Common AD DS attacks and mitigations**
- **Pass-the-hash / pass-the-ticket**: reuse of cached credentials. Mitigate with tiered logon restrictions, **Credential Guard**, **Windows LAPS**, Protected Users, and no Tier 0 logons on workstations.
- **Kerberoasting**: requesting service tickets for accounts with SPNs and cracking them offline. Mitigate with **gMSA** or 25+ character passwords and AES-only encryption.
- **AS-REP roasting**: accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication. Require pre-auth.
- **DCSync / DCShadow**: abuse of replication rights. Restrict replication permissions to DCs; detect with **Defender for Identity**.
- **Golden Ticket**: forged TGTs signed with the **krbtgt** key. Protect DCs as Tier 0; reset krbtgt twice after compromise.
- **AD CS abuse (ESC-style)**: misconfigured templates allow requesting certificates as any user. Review templates and enrolment rights; monitor AD CS with MDI sensors.
- **Password spray / brute force**: fine-grained password policies, smart lockout, and MFA on remote access.

**Governance**
- Regular reviews of privileged groups and **lateral movement paths** (shown in Defender for Identity).
- Identity security posture assessments in **Microsoft Secure Score / Exposure Management**.
- Resilience: protected offline DC backups, documented **AD forest recovery**, and the ability to operate if Entra Connect or AD FS is lost.

terms.d: Offline cracking of service tickets for accounts with service principal names.
Abusing directory replication rights to pull password hashes from a DC.
Forged Kerberos TGT made with the stolen krbtgt key.
Chain of sessions and admin rights an attacker could follow to sensitive accounts.

lessons.trap: Resetting the krbtgt password once doesn't invalidate a Golden Ticket because the previous key is still accepted; it must be reset twice (with replication time between).
lessons.example: Defender for Identity flags a lateral movement path from a helpdesk PC to a Domain Admin; the fix is removing the admin's interactive sessions on Tier 2 devices.

lessons.title: Secure administration of cloud tenants, SaaS and multicloud
lessons.short: Secure tenant administration uses cloud-only admin accounts, phishing-resistant MFA, PIM, emergency access accounts, protected actions and admin portals reached only from PAWs. In multicloud and SaaS, federate admin access to Entra ID and monitor admin activity centrally.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft 365 and Entra tenant**
- **Cloud-only** accounts for Entra privileged roles (not synced from AD DS, so an on-premises compromise can't take over the cloud).
- Fewer than five Global Administrators; at least **two emergency access accounts** excluded from most CA but protected with FIDO2 and monitored with alerts.
- **PIM** for all privileged roles; **phishing-resistant MFA** authentication strength for admin roles.
- **Protected actions** for CA policy changes, cross-tenant settings and hard deletes.
- Restrict access to admin portals and Microsoft Graph PowerShell; review **app consent** and high-privilege app permissions.

**Azure**
- Management group hierarchy with least-privilege RBAC; PIM for Owner/User Access Administrator; **Azure Policy** guardrails; Activity log to Sentinel.

**Multicloud and SaaS**
- Federate AWS IAM Identity Center and Google Cloud admin access to Entra ID; avoid AWS root and long-lived IAM user keys.
- Use **Defender for Cloud** CSPM/CIEM for AWS and GCP posture and over-permissioned identities.
- Use **Defender for Cloud Apps** SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM) and app connectors for admin activity in Salesforce, ServiceNow and others.
- MSPs use **GDAP** (granular delegated admin privileges) for Microsoft 365 customer tenants and **Azure Lighthouse** for Azure.

terms.d: Granular delegated admin privileges: least-privilege, time-bound partner access to customer tenants.
Privileged account created in Entra ID, not synced from AD DS.
SaaS security posture management, for example in Defender for Cloud Apps.

lessons.trap: Syncing on-premises Domain Admins to be Global Administrators is wrong; cloud privileged roles should be held by cloud-only accounts.
lessons.example: An MSP moves from legacy DAP to GDAP with time-bound Helpdesk Administrator access, and the customer's Global Administrators are cloud-only accounts with FIDO2 keys.

lessons.title: Cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM)
lessons.short: CIEM finds and right-sizes excessive permissions held by human and workload identities across Azure, AWS and GCP. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management was retired in 2025; Microsoft now provides CIEM in the Defender CSPM plan of Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
lessons.deep:
In multicloud, identities accumulate permissions they never use: an AWS role with `*:*`, a GCP service account with Owner, an Azure service principal with Contributor on a subscription. **CIEM** (cloud infrastructure entitlement management) addresses this gap between **granted** and **used** permissions.

Capabilities to design for:
- **Discovery** of identities and entitlements across Azure (Entra users, groups, service principals), AWS (IAM users, roles, groups) and GCP (IAM users, groups, service accounts).
- **Usage analytics**: compare granted permissions with activity to find **overprovisioned** and **inactive** identities.
- **Recommendations**: remove inactive or guest identities with access, limit admin privileges, right-size roles, enforce MFA for IAM users.
- **Attack path** context: an over-permissioned identity combined with an exposed VM appears in **attack path analysis** and **cloud security explorer**.

**Product status (verify dates in questions carefully)**
- **Microsoft Entra Permissions Management** was retired: no longer sold from April 2025, support ended **1 October 2025**.
- Microsoft recommends **Defender CSPM** in Defender for Cloud for CIEM; third-party CIEM tools are an option for deeper needs.

Pair CIEM with PIM for Azure roles and federated, time-bound access in AWS and GCP.

terms.d: Cloud infrastructure entitlement management: discovering and right-sizing cloud permissions.
Identity granted far more permissions than it uses.
Paid Defender for Cloud posture plan including CIEM, attack paths and cloud security explorer.

lessons.trap: Recommending a new deployment of Microsoft Entra Permissions Management is wrong after its retirement; the current Microsoft answer is Defender CSPM.
lessons.example: Defender CSPM shows a GCP service account with Owner that has only read from one bucket in 90 days; the team replaces Owner with a custom read-only role.

lessons.title: Evaluating access review solutions
lessons.short: Access reviews periodically ask reviewers to confirm whether users, guests or service principals still need group, app, access package or privileged role access. Evaluate scope, reviewers, recurrence, decision helpers and auto-apply results against compliance requirements.
lessons.deep:
**What can be reviewed**
- Group and Microsoft 365 group/Teams membership, application assignments, **access package assignments**, **Entra roles and Azure resource roles in PIM**, and (Governance) PIM for Groups and catalog reviews.

**Design choices**
- **Reviewers**: resource owners, managers, selected users, or **self-review**. Multi-stage reviews add a second stage, for example manager then app owner.
- **Scope**: all users, guests only, or (Governance) inactive users only.
- **Recurrence**: weekly to annually; duration of each instance.
- **Decision helpers**: last sign-in recommendations; machine-learning-assisted recommendations based on peer similarity (Governance).
- **Upon completion**: **auto-apply results** to remove denied users; action if reviewers don't respond (remove access, approve, take recommendations).
- For guests: block sign-in for 30 days then delete when removed from all access.

**Licensing**: Entra ID P2 for core reviews; Entra ID Governance for ML-assisted, inactive-user-only and PIM for Groups reviews.

**Evaluating fit**: Microsoft-native reviews cover Entra-integrated resources. For non-Entra resources, use custom data provided resource reviews or a third-party IGA solution, and Defender for Cloud CIEM for cloud infrastructure permissions.

Audit evidence: review history and downloadable results support SOX, ISO 27001 and similar audits.

terms.d: Recurring attestation of who should keep access to a resource.
Setting that removes denied access automatically when a review ends.
Review with sequential reviewer stages.
Users attest to their own continued need for access.

lessons.trap: Without auto-apply, denied decisions aren't enforced automatically; an answer that 'creates a review' but never applies results misses the requirement.
lessons.example: A quarterly multi-stage review of the payments app uses managers then app owners, removes non-responders, and auto-applies results to satisfy SOX evidence.

lessons.title: Privileged access workstations (PAW)
lessons.short: A privileged access workstation is a hardened, Intune-managed device used only for administration: no email or general browsing, application control enforced, no local admin, and hardware-backed security. Microsoft defines enterprise, specialized and privileged device profiles.
lessons.deep:
Admins are only as secure as the device they type on. Microsoft's **device security profiles**:
- **Enterprise**: standard productivity device with Defender for Endpoint and security baselines.
- **Specialized**: no local admin, only admin-deployed apps (application control enforced), email and browsing still allowed.
- **Privileged (PAW)**: highest protection for roles whose compromise would materially harm the organization.

**PAW requirements**
- **Email and general web browsing blocked**; deny-by-default URL allow list.
- Managed by **Intune** with security baselines and **Defender for Endpoint**; deployed with **Windows Autopilot** to a known-good state; no BYOD.
- **Application control** (AppLocker/App Control for Business) enforced; apps only via Intune.
- **No local admin rights**.
- Hardware root of trust: **TPM 2.0**, UEFI Secure Boot, virtualization-based security, **Credential Guard**, BitLocker.
- Separate admin account; admins use a different device or account for productivity.

**Enforcing PAW use**: a Conditional Access policy with a **device filter** (for example, extensionAttribute or a PAW device group) or compliant-device requirement for admin roles; combine with PIM authentication context and protected actions.

Cloud PCs (Windows 365) can be configured as privileged workstations where physical PAWs are impractical, if hardened to the same profile.

terms.d: Privileged access workstation: hardened device dedicated to administrative tasks.
Locked-down device without local admin that still allows email and browsing.
Conditional Access condition targeting devices by attributes such as extensionAttribute1.
Cloud-based provisioning that resets new devices to a managed, known-good state.

lessons.trap: A PAW that still allows Outlook and web browsing is a specialized device, not a PAW; and a jump server alone doesn't protect credentials typed on an unmanaged laptop.
lessons.example: Global Administrators can activate roles only from devices with extensionAttribute1 = 'PAW', enforced by a Conditional Access device filter.

lessons.title: Secure remote administration: Bastion and just-in-time VM access
lessons.short: Remote administration should never expose RDP or SSH to the internet. Use Azure Bastion for browser or native-client RDP/SSH over TLS without public IPs, just-in-time VM access in Defender for Servers Plan 2 to open ports briefly, and Entra Private Access for on-premises servers.
lessons.deep:
**Azure Bastion**
- Managed PaaS deployed in the VNet's **AzureBastionSubnet**; admins connect over TLS 443 from the Azure portal or native client, and target VMs need **no public IP**.
- **Standard/Premium** SKUs add native client support, shareable links, IP-based connections and, on Premium, **session recording**.
- Combine with Entra ID sign-in to VMs and Conditional Access.

**Just-in-time (JIT) VM access**
- Part of **Defender for Servers Plan 2**.
- Locks management ports (3389, 22) with NSG or Azure Firewall rules; an approved request opens the port for a time window and only from the requester's IP.
- Requests are logged in the Activity log.

**On-premises and other clouds**
- **Microsoft Entra Private Access** gives per-app access to RDP/SSH targets with Conditional Access, replacing VPN.
- Admin access always from a **PAW**, possibly via a hardened **jump server** in the same tier.

**Design principles**: no inbound management ports from the internet; identity-based, time-bound access; recorded sessions for privileged work; separate management subnets with NSGs.

terms.d: Managed RDP/SSH broker over TLS so VMs need no public IP.
Defender for Servers Plan 2 feature that opens management ports only on approved request.
Dedicated subnet name required for Azure Bastion.

lessons.trap: JIT VM access needs Defender for Servers Plan 2, not Plan 1; and Bastion removes the need for public IPs on VMs, not the need for a PAW.
lessons.example: Ops engineers connect to production VMs only through Bastion Premium with session recording, from PAWs, after activating their PIM role.

lessons.title: Translating compliance requirements into security controls
lessons.short: Architects turn regulatory clauses into concrete, testable controls: identify the obligation, map it to a control framework such as the Microsoft cloud security benchmark or NIST, assign responsibility under the shared responsibility model, implement with technical tools, and collect evidence.
lessons.deep:
A regulation says *what* (for example, 'protect cardholder data', 'log access to personal data', 'keep data in the EU'). Architects design *how*.

**Method**
1. **Inventory obligations**: laws (GDPR, HIPAA), industry standards (PCI DSS), frameworks (ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53), contracts and internal policy.
2. **Map to a control framework**: the **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)** maps to CIS, NIST and PCI DSS controls; Compliance Manager templates map regulations to improvement actions.
3. **Assign responsibility**: under the **shared responsibility model**, some controls are Microsoft-managed (physical security), some customer-managed (MFA, data classification), some shared.
4. **Implement technical controls**, for example:
   - Data residency -> Azure Policy *Allowed locations*.
   - Encryption -> customer-managed keys in Key Vault/Managed HSM.
   - Access logging -> Purview Audit, diagnostic settings to Sentinel.
   - Data protection -> sensitivity labels, DLP, retention.
   - Least privilege -> PIM, access reviews.
5. **Measure and evidence**: Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard, Compliance Manager scores, audit reports, Microsoft Service Trust Portal for Microsoft's own audit reports (SOC, ISO).

Write controls so they are **testable**: 'All storage accounts deny public network access' is testable; 'data is secure' is not.

terms.d: Microsoft's multicloud security control framework, mapped to CIS, NIST and PCI DSS.
Division of security duties between cloud provider and customer by service type.
Microsoft site with its own audit reports and compliance documents.
Requirement that data is stored in specific geographic locations.

lessons.trap: Microsoft's ISO certificate doesn't make your workload compliant; customer-managed controls still need implementation and evidence.
lessons.example: A GDPR 'data must stay in the EU' clause becomes an Azure Policy Allowed locations assignment (West Europe, North Europe) with deny effect at the EU management group.

lessons.title: Compliance solutions with Microsoft Purview
lessons.short: Microsoft Purview delivers compliance through Compliance Manager (assessments, compliance score, improvement actions), Information Protection and DLP, Data Lifecycle and Records Management, Audit, eDiscovery, Communication Compliance and Insider Risk Management.
lessons.deep:
**Compliance Manager**
- Over 360 **regulatory templates** (ISO 27001, NIST, GDPR, HIPAA and more) and custom templates to create **assessments**.
- Each assessment lists **Microsoft-managed**, **customer-managed** and **shared** controls.
- **Improvement actions** can be assigned, evidenced and tracked; points roll up to a **compliance score** (risk-based). The default starting assessment is the **Data Protection Baseline**.
- Some templates are included by licence; premium templates may need add-ons.

**Other Purview solutions mapped to requirements**
- **Information Protection**: sensitivity labels (encryption, marking), auto-labelling. 
- **Data Loss Prevention**: policies for Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, endpoints and more.
- **Data Lifecycle Management / Records Management**: retention policies and labels, disposition review, regulatory records.
- **Audit (Standard/Premium)** and **eDiscovery** for investigations and legal hold.
- **Communication Compliance** and **Insider Risk Management** for conduct and insider threats.
- **DSPM for AI** for AI-related data risk (Copilot and other AI apps).
- **Data Map / Unified Catalog** to discover and classify data across Azure, on-premises and multicloud sources.

Architect focus: pick the solution that produces the required **evidence** and **enforcement**, not just visibility.

terms.d: Purview tool for assessments, improvement actions and compliance score.
Recommended step that implements a control and earns score points.
Purview label that keeps or deletes content and can declare records.
Risk-weighted measure of progress on improvement actions.

lessons.trap: Compliance score is a measure of progress, not a certification of compliance; and Microsoft-managed controls are already scored for you.
lessons.example: A health insurer creates a HIPAA assessment in Compliance Manager, assigns improvement actions to owners, and uses retention labels plus DLP for PHI to close them.

lessons.title: Azure Policy for security and compliance
lessons.short: Azure Policy evaluates Azure resources against rules and enforces them with effects such as deny, audit, modify and deployIfNotExists. Group policies into initiatives, assign at management group scope, use exemptions sparingly, and use remediation tasks with managed identities to fix existing resources.
lessons.deep:
**Building blocks**
- **Policy definition**: a rule (`if` condition, `then` effect).
- **Initiative (policy set)**: a group of definitions, such as the MCSB initiative or a regulatory initiative (ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53).
- **Assignment** at management group, subscription or resource group scope, with parameters and exclusions.
- **Exemptions**: *waiver* or *mitigated*, optionally time-limited.

**Effects**
- **deny**: blocks non-compliant creates/updates.
- **audit** / **auditIfNotExists**: report only.
- **modify** / **append**: change the request (for example, add tags).
- **deployIfNotExists (DINE)**: deploy a related resource (for example, diagnostic settings, an agent). DINE and modify need a **managed identity** on the assignment.
- **denyAction**: block specific actions such as delete.
- **manual**: attestation for controls that can't be checked automatically.
- **disabled**.

**Design guidance**
- Assign guardrails at the **management group** level (Azure landing zones), so new subscriptions inherit them.
- Start with **audit**, then move to **deny** once impact is known.
- **Remediation tasks** fix existing resources for DINE/modify.
- Store definitions as code (policy as code with CI/CD).
- Azure Policy covers Azure Resource Manager, Arc-enabled servers (machine configuration) and AKS (Azure Policy for Kubernetes / Gatekeeper).

terms.d: Set of policy definitions assigned and tracked together.
Effect that deploys a related resource when it's missing; needs a managed identity.
Applies DINE or modify to existing non-compliant resources.
Excludes a scope from an assignment as a waiver or mitigated, with optional expiry.

lessons.trap: New assignments with deployIfNotExists don't fix existing resources automatically; you need a remediation task. And audit doesn't prevent anything.
lessons.example: The platform team assigns 'Storage accounts should disable public network access' with deny at the Landing Zones management group and a DINE policy that sends Key Vault logs to the Sentinel workspace.

lessons.title: Validating regulatory alignment with Defender for Cloud
lessons.short: Defender for Cloud's regulatory compliance dashboard measures Azure, AWS and GCP resources against standards. The Microsoft cloud security benchmark is applied by default; adding other standards needs a paid Defender plan, and custom standards need Defender CSPM. Manual attestation covers controls that can't be checked automatically.
lessons.deep:
**Regulatory compliance dashboard**
- **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)** is enabled automatically when Defender for Cloud is enabled on a subscription, and applies across Azure, AWS and GCP.
- Connecting AWS also enables the **AWS Foundational Security Best Practices** standard; GCP enables the **GCP Default** benchmark.
- Add standards such as **PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, SOC 2, HIPAA/HITRUST**: requires at least one paid Defender plan (not Defender for Servers Plan 1 or Defender for APIs Plan 1). **Custom standards** require **Defender CSPM**.
- Assigning a standard requires **Owner** or **Resource Policy Contributor** on the scope.

**Reading results**
- Each control shows **passing** (green), **failing** (red) or **not available** (grey: procedural, platform-owned or not automatically assessable).
- Use **manual attestation** to add evidence for procedural controls.
- Drill into failing assessments -> recommendations -> affected resources -> remediation (often a **Fix** or Azure Policy DINE).

**Validate and report**
- Download compliance reports, export continuously to Log Analytics or Event Hubs (continuous export), and use workbooks.
- **Secure Score** tracks posture; the compliance dashboard tracks a standard. Neither proves certification by itself.
- Map Defender for Cloud results into **Compliance Manager** for a single compliance view across Microsoft 365 and cloud.

terms.d: Defender for Cloud view of control status against chosen standards.
Recording evidence for controls that can't be assessed automatically.
Streams Defender for Cloud alerts, recommendations and compliance data to Log Analytics or Event Hubs.
Posture metric based on resolved security recommendations.

lessons.trap: Free foundational CSPM gives MCSB only; to show PCI DSS or ISO 27001 you need a paid Defender plan, and custom standards need Defender CSPM.
lessons.example: A fintech enables Defender CSPM, adds PCI DSS v4 to its payment subscriptions and AWS account, fixes failing network controls, and attests manually to its incident response procedures.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud and the MCSB
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP). Its posture assessments are driven by the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB), which is assigned by default and turned into security recommendations across Azure, AWS and GCP.
lessons.deep:
Defender for Cloud combines three things: **cloud security posture management (CSPM)**, **cloud workload protection (CWPP)** and **DevOps security**. As an architect you use it to answer "how well configured are we?" across every cloud.

The yardstick is the **Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB)**. It is Microsoft's own set of security controls, grouped into domains such as Network Security (NS), Identity Management (IM), Privileged Access (PA), Data Protection (DP), Logging and Threat Detection (LT) and Posture and Vulnerability Management (PV). Each control maps to industry frameworks such as **CIS Controls, NIST and PCI-DSS**, and MCSB covers Azure plus AWS and GCP guidance. Version 2 (preview) adds an AI security domain.

When you enable Defender for Cloud on a subscription, MCSB is the **default standard**: its Azure Policy definitions evaluate resources and produce **recommendations**, which feed **secure score**. The **regulatory compliance dashboard** shows MCSB status, and you can add further standards (for example PCI DSS or ISO 27001), which needs a paid plan such as Defender CSPM.

Microsoft also publishes a **security baseline** for each Azure service, which applies the MCSB controls to that one service (for example, the baseline for Azure Key Vault).

terms.d: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark: Microsoft's multicloud set of security controls, the default standard in Defender for Cloud.
Cloud-native application protection platform: CSPM, CWPP and DevOps security in one product.
Defender for Cloud view showing pass/fail of controls for MCSB and any added standards.
MCSB guidance applied to one specific Azure service.

lessons.trap: Candidates pick CIS or NIST as the default standard; in Defender for Cloud the default is always MCSB, and other standards are added on top.
lessons.example: An auditor asks for PCI DSS evidence across Azure and AWS: the architect enables Defender CSPM, adds the PCI DSS standard, and exports the regulatory compliance report.

lessons.title: Microsoft Secure Score and cloud secure score
lessons.short: Microsoft Secure Score measures Microsoft 365, identity, endpoint and SaaS posture in the Defender portal. Defender for Cloud has its own secure score for cloud resources: a classic control-based score and a risk-based Cloud Secure Score. The scores are calculated differently and are not comparable.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft Secure Score** lives in the Microsoft Defender portal (under Exposure Management). It covers products such as Microsoft Entra ID, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, Defender for Office 365, Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint and connected SaaS apps through Defender for Cloud Apps. Each **recommended action** is worth 10 points or less; most are all-or-nothing, but some give **partial points** by coverage (50 of 100 users with MFA on a 10-point action = 5 points).

Statuses: **To address**, **Planned**, **Risk accepted** (no points), **Resolved through third party** and **Resolved through alternate mitigation** (both award points, unverified by Microsoft), and **Completed** (set by Microsoft when it detects the control).

**Defender for Cloud secure score (classic)** is built from MCSB recommendations grouped into **security controls**. You only earn a control's points when **all** its recommendations are remediated for a resource; **preview recommendations are excluded**. It is viewable per subscription, connector or management group.

The newer **Cloud Secure Score** (Defender portal, Exposure Management) is **risk-based**, 0-100, weighting recommendations by risk level, **asset risk factors** (internet exposure, data sensitivity) and **asset criticality**.

terms.d: A Secure Score item worth up to 10 points, some with partial credit.
Secure Score status recording a decision not to act; it earns no points.
Group of related Defender for Cloud recommendations; points are earned only when all are fixed.
Risk-based 0-100 cloud score that factors in asset risk and criticality.

lessons.trap: Expect a question on statuses: 'Risk accepted' gives no points, while 'Resolved through third party' does; and partial remediation of a Defender for Cloud control earns nothing.
lessons.example: A company uses a non-Microsoft mail gateway that already covers a recommended action, so the admin marks it 'Resolved through third party' and the points are added.

lessons.title: Integrated hybrid and multicloud posture
lessons.short: Defender for Cloud gives one posture view across Azure, AWS, GCP, on-premises (through Azure Arc) and DevOps platforms. Foundational CSPM is free; Defender CSPM adds attack paths, cloud security explorer, governance rules, agentless scanning, data and AI posture.
lessons.deep:
An integrated design brings every environment into one Defender for Cloud tenant view:
- **AWS**: an environment connector, deployed with a CloudFormation template or Terraform that creates IAM roles trusted by Microsoft Entra ID (no stored long-lived keys). Connecting the **management account** auto-provisions connectors for existing and new member accounts.
- **GCP**: a connector at project or organization level.
- **On-premises and other clouds' servers**: **Azure Arc**.
- **DevOps**: GitHub, Azure DevOps and GitLab connectors for code and IaC findings.

**Foundational CSPM (free)**: asset inventory, MCSB recommendations, secure score, remediation tools, workflow automation, workbooks and data export.

**Defender CSPM (paid)** adds: attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, risk prioritization, governance rules, regulatory compliance standards, agentless VM vulnerability and secrets scanning, data security posture (sensitive data discovery), EASM insights, AI security posture, API posture and **code-to-cloud** mapping.

Design tips: enable at **management group** scope so new subscriptions inherit plans, use **governance rules** to assign owners and due dates, and pipe recommendations to the Defender portal or Sentinel for one operations view.

terms.d: Defender for Cloud object linking an AWS account, GCP project or DevOps org.
Free posture tier: inventory, MCSB recommendations, secure score.
Paid posture plan with attack paths, explorer, agentless scanning, DSPM and AI-SPM.
Defender CSPM feature that assigns owners and due dates to recommendations at scale.

lessons.trap: Exam scenarios that need attack paths, code-to-cloud or sensitive-data context require Defender CSPM, not the free Foundational CSPM.
lessons.example: A retailer with 140 AWS accounts connects the AWS management account once, and new member accounts appear in Defender for Cloud automatically.

lessons.title: CWPP: Defender for Servers Plan 1 vs Plan 2
lessons.short: Defender for Servers protects Windows and Linux machines in Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises. Plan 1 centres on Defender for Endpoint EDR; Plan 2 adds agentless scanning, premium vulnerability management, file integrity monitoring, just-in-time VM access and a 500 MB per node per day data allowance.
lessons.deep:
Cloud workload protection (CWPP) plans add threat protection on top of posture. For servers you choose:

**Plan 1**: integrates **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** (EDR, next-generation antivirus) and basic vulnerability findings. It can be enabled on a whole subscription **or on individual resources**.

**Plan 2**: everything in Plan 1 plus:
- **Agentless scanning** of disks for vulnerabilities, malware and secrets
- **Premium Defender Vulnerability Management**
- **File integrity monitoring (FIM)** of files and registry
- **Just-in-time (JIT) VM access** to keep management ports closed until requested
- **OS configuration assessment** against MCSB compute baselines and OS update assessment
- **Free data ingestion of 500 MB per node per day** (pooled across machines) for security tables such as SecurityEvent
- Network map and, for new subscriptions, Defender for DNS coverage

Plan 2 is enabled at subscription level (it cannot be switched on per resource, only off). Non-Azure servers are covered through **Azure Arc**, which the AWS and GCP connectors can auto-provision.

terms.d: Opens RDP/SSH ports only for an approved user, source IP and time window.
File integrity monitoring: tracks changes to OS files and registry keys.
Snapshot-based disk scanning for vulnerabilities, malware and secrets without an agent.
Plan 2 allowance of 500 MB/node/day free ingestion for listed security tables.

lessons.trap: JIT, FIM and the 500 MB ingestion benefit are Plan 2 only; scenarios asking for EDR alone at lowest cost point to Plan 1.
lessons.example: Production VMs need FIM for PCI DSS, so production gets Plan 2 while a lab subscription needing only EDR gets Plan 1.

lessons.title: CWPP: choosing the other Defender plans
lessons.short: Beyond servers, Defender for Cloud has workload plans for Storage, databases (Azure SQL, SQL servers on machines, open-source relational, Cosmos DB), Containers, App Service, Key Vault, Resource Manager, APIs and AI services. Pick the plan that matches the resource you must protect.
lessons.deep:
Choosing CWPP is a mapping exercise: workload type to plan.
- **Defender for Storage**: detects suspicious access, malware uploads (malware scanning), sensitive data threat detection and SAS token misuse on storage accounts.
- **Defender for Databases**: separate plans for **Azure SQL Databases**, **SQL servers on machines** (SQL Server on Azure VMs, or on-premises and other clouds through Azure Arc), **open-source relational databases** (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB) and **Azure Cosmos DB**. They give vulnerability assessment (SQL) and threat detection such as SQL injection.
- **Defender for Containers**: Kubernetes and container protection in Azure, AWS and GCP.
- **Defender for App Service**: attacks against web apps on App Service.
- **Defender for Key Vault**: unusual or harmful access to vaults.
- **Defender for Resource Manager**: suspicious management operations (control-plane activity) through Azure Resource Manager.
- **Defender for APIs**: posture and threat detection for APIs published in Azure API Management.
- **Defender for AI Services**: runtime threats to generative AI applications.

Alerts from all plans flow to Defender XDR incidents and can be streamed to Microsoft Sentinel.

terms.d: Detects suspicious control-plane operations against Azure Resource Manager.
Defender for Storage feature that scans uploaded blobs for malware.
Defender plan for SQL Server on VMs, including on-premises via Azure Arc.

lessons.trap: SQL Server running on a VM or on-premises needs 'SQL servers on machines', not 'Azure SQL Databases'; ARM-level abuse is Resource Manager, not Key Vault.
lessons.example: A partner portal lets customers upload documents to Blob Storage, so the architect enables Defender for Storage malware scanning on that account.

lessons.title: Hybrid and multicloud integration with Azure Arc
lessons.short: Azure Arc projects servers, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances outside Azure into Azure Resource Manager. Once Arc-enabled, they can be governed with Azure Policy, protected by Defender for Cloud, patched with Azure Update Manager and monitored like native resources.
lessons.deep:
**Azure Arc-enabled servers** use the **Azure Connected Machine agent** on Windows or Linux machines on-premises or in another cloud. The machine gets an **Azure resource ID**, sits in a resource group, and can be tagged and controlled with Azure RBAC. It also receives a system-assigned **managed identity**.

What Arc unlocks for security:
- **Defender for Servers** (and Defender for Endpoint) protection and secure score recommendations
- **Azure Policy machine configuration** to audit or apply OS settings
- **Azure Update Manager** for patching, **Azure Monitor Agent** for logs into Sentinel
- Defender for SQL on Arc-enabled SQL Server

Arc is only for machines **outside Azure**; Azure VMs do not need it. The AWS and GCP connectors in Defender for Cloud can **auto-provision the Arc agent** on EC2 and Compute Engine instances.

Connectivity is outbound HTTPS; for private connectivity use an **Azure Arc Private Link Scope** with private endpoints over ExpressRoute or VPN. The agent sends a heartbeat every five minutes; a machine disconnected for 45 days can expire and must be reconnected.

**Arc-enabled Kubernetes** lets Defender for Containers and Azure Policy reach non-AKS clusters.

terms.d: Agent that registers a non-Azure server as an Arc resource.
Resource that lets Arc agents reach Azure over private endpoints.
Azure Policy feature that audits/configures settings inside the OS.

lessons.trap: Arc is the answer when non-Azure servers need Azure Policy or Defender for Servers; it is never used for Azure VMs.
lessons.example: A bank's VMware servers are Arc-enabled so Defender for Servers Plan 2 and machine configuration baselines apply exactly as they do to Azure VMs.

lessons.title: Defender External Attack Surface Management
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (EASM) discovers your internet-facing assets from the outside, starting from discovery seeds, and keeps an inventory of domains, IP blocks, hosts, ASNs, email contacts and Whois organizations so you can find unknown and unmanaged exposure.
lessons.deep:
Attackers see you from the internet, not from your CMDB. **Defender EASM** recreates that view.

**How it works**: you provide **discovery seeds** (known domains, IP blocks, hosts, ASNs, Whois organizations). Microsoft's discovery engine recursively follows connections from those seeds to infer related infrastructure, including shadow IT and forgotten sites.

**Inventory states** label each asset:
- **Approved Inventory**: owned by you, your responsibility
- **Candidate**: related to seeds but not confirmed; needs review
- **Dependency**: third-party infrastructure your assets rely on
- **Monitor Only**: relevant but not controlled (for example, a franchisee)
- **Requires Investigation**: confidence scores suggest a link that needs manual validation

**Dashboards** surface vulnerabilities (CVEs on exposed hosts), expiring certificates, compliance (for example, OWASP-type findings) and hygiene issues.

Design points: Defender EASM is an Azure resource with Owner/Contributor/Reader access; **cross-tenant access, including Azure Lighthouse, is not supported**. Its findings also enrich **Defender CSPM** (internet exposure) and **Microsoft Security Exposure Management**.

terms.d: Known asset used as the starting point for external discovery.
EASM state for assets you own and must secure.
EASM state for related assets whose ownership is not yet confirmed.
Third-party infrastructure that supports your owned assets.

lessons.trap: Don't confuse EASM (outside-in discovery of unknown internet assets) with attack path analysis (inside-out graph of known cloud resources).
lessons.example: After an acquisition, the architect seeds EASM with the acquired company's domains and finds an unpatched VPN portal nobody had listed.

lessons.title: Attack paths and cloud security explorer
lessons.short: Defender CSPM builds a cloud security graph of assets, identities, network exposure and vulnerabilities. Attack path analysis finds exploitable routes from an internet-facing entry point to critical assets; cloud security explorer lets you query the same graph for custom risks.
lessons.deep:
Isolated recommendations do not show how weaknesses chain together. The **cloud security graph** in Defender CSPM links resources, permissions, network connections, internet exposure, vulnerabilities and sensitive data.

**Attack path analysis** scans that graph for:
1. an **entry point** (for example an internet-exposed VM with an exploitable vulnerability)
2. **lateral movement** steps (an attached managed identity with rights on another resource)
3. a **target** (a critical asset such as a storage account holding sensitive data)

Paths are ranked by risk factors such as internet exposure, permissions and lateral movement, and come with remediation that **breaks the path**. Coverage includes VMs, containers, storage, serverless, APIs, repositories and AI resources.

**Cloud security explorer** is the query builder for proactive risk hunting: you build graph queries such as "internet-exposed VMs with high-severity vulnerabilities that can authenticate to a key vault".

Requirements: **Defender CSPM**, plus either **agentless scanning for VMs** or the Defender for Servers vulnerability assessment. Microsoft Security Exposure Management extends attack paths across hybrid identity and endpoints and highlights **choke points** where many paths converge.

terms.d: Context graph of assets, identities, exposure and vulnerabilities in Defender CSPM.
Externally reachable, exploitable weakness where an attack path begins.
Node where many attack paths converge; fixing it breaks many paths.
Query builder for custom graph-based risk hunting.

lessons.trap: Attack path analysis is automatic and prebuilt; for an ad hoc question about your own risk combination, the answer is cloud security explorer.
lessons.example: An attack path shows an internet-facing VM with a critical CVE whose managed identity can read a customer-data storage account; removing the role assignment breaks the path.

lessons.title: Exposure Management initiatives, insights and attack surface reduction
lessons.short: Microsoft Security Exposure Management unifies posture across endpoints, identities, cloud, SaaS and external surface. Security initiatives track scored programmes such as Ransomware Protection or Zero Trust; exposure insights, the attack surface map and critical asset management help prioritise. Attack surface reduction rules shrink endpoint exposure.
lessons.deep:
Posture work must be a repeatable **process**, not a one-off scan. **Microsoft Security Exposure Management** (in the Defender portal) supports a continuous threat exposure management cycle:
- **Security initiatives**: scored programmes for a domain or threat, for example **Cloud Security**, **SaaS Security**, **Identity Security**, **Ransomware Protection**, **Business Email Compromise** and **Zero Trust**. Each has **metrics** and **recommendations** so leaders can track progress over time.
- **Exposure insights**: aggregated posture data and context about assets.
- **Attack surface map** and **attack paths** across on-premises, hybrid and cloud, with **choke points**.
- **Critical asset management**: predefined and custom classifications of crown-jewel devices, identities and cloud resources, used to prioritise.
- Third-party data connectors (for example ServiceNow CMDB, Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7).

**Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules** in Defender for Endpoint block risky behaviours such as Office apps creating child processes or credential stealing from LSASS. Roll them out in **Audit** mode first, then **Block** (or **Warn** where users may override).

Exposure Management is available in the public cloud only, not in US Gov or China sovereign clouds.

terms.d: Scored programme in Exposure Management with metrics and recommendations.
Classifying crown-jewel assets so exposures on them are prioritised.
Defender for Endpoint rules blocking risky behaviours; modes Audit, Block, Warn.
Continuous threat exposure management: scope, discover, prioritise, validate, mobilise.

lessons.trap: Leadership-level 'track our readiness against ransomware over time' maps to an Exposure Management security initiative, not a compliance dashboard.
lessons.example: The CISO reviews the Ransomware Protection initiative score monthly while the endpoint team moves ASR rules from Audit to Block.

lessons.title: Server security requirements across platforms
lessons.short: Server requirements should be the same whatever the OS or location: onboard to Defender for Endpoint through Defender for Servers, harden against a baseline, patch, restrict management access with JIT or Azure Bastion, and bring non-Azure servers in through Azure Arc.
lessons.deep:
An architect writes requirements, not click-paths. A good cross-platform server specification covers:
- **Protection**: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Windows Server and Linux, deployed through **Defender for Servers** so onboarding is automatic for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled machines (AWS, GCP, on-premises).
- **Vulnerability management**: Defender Vulnerability Management findings or agentless scanning (Plan 2) and a patch SLA delivered with **Azure Update Manager**.
- **Hardening**: an OS baseline (MCSB compute baseline through **Azure Policy machine configuration**, CIS, or Group Policy from the Security Compliance Toolkit).
- **Management access**: no public RDP/SSH; use **just-in-time VM access** or **Azure Bastion**, and privileged access workstations for admins. Linux should use SSH keys or Microsoft Entra ID login rather than passwords.
- **Identity**: managed identities instead of stored secrets; Windows LAPS for local admin passwords.
- **Monitoring**: Azure Monitor Agent sending security events to Microsoft Sentinel; file integrity monitoring where regulations require it.
- **Resilience**: backups (Azure Backup with soft delete and immutability).

The point: one standard, applied through one control plane (Azure Resource Manager via Arc), so posture is measured the same way everywhere.

terms.d: Managed PaaS for browser-based RDP/SSH to VMs without public IPs.
Service for assessing and deploying OS updates on Azure and Arc machines.
Sign in to Azure Linux VMs with Entra ID credentials governed by RBAC and Conditional Access.

lessons.trap: When the stem says 'no public management ports', the answer is JIT or Azure Bastion, not simply an NSG rule that allows RDP from the internet.
lessons.example: A design standard requires every Linux and Windows server, wherever it runs, to be Arc-enabled or in Azure, onboarded to Defender for Servers, and reachable only through Bastion.

lessons.title: Mobile devices and clients
lessons.short: Use Microsoft Intune for device compliance and app protection, Defender for Endpoint for mobile threat defence, and Conditional Access to enforce both. Corporate devices are enrolled (MDM); personal devices can use app protection policies (MAM) without enrolment.
lessons.deep:
Client requirements depend on ownership:
- **Corporate-owned**: enrol in **Intune (MDM)**, for example Windows Autopilot, Apple Automated Device Enrollment, or Android Enterprise fully managed. Apply **compliance policies** (encryption, OS version, passcode, jailbreak/root detection) and configuration profiles.
- **Personal (BYOD)**: avoid controlling the whole device. Use **Intune app protection policies (MAM)** that protect corporate data inside apps such as Outlook and Teams: block copy-paste to personal apps, require a PIN, and allow **selective wipe** of corporate data only. Android Enterprise **work profile** is a middle ground.
- **Mobile threat defence**: **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on iOS/Android** detects phishing sites, malicious apps and risky networks; its device risk level can feed Intune compliance.

Enforcement is in **Conditional Access**: grant controls **Require device to be marked as compliant**, or **Require app protection policy**. Add **authentication strengths** such as phishing-resistant MFA.

Clients (Windows/macOS) also need disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault), EDR, ASR rules and a security baseline.

terms.d: Intune policy that protects corporate data inside apps, with or without device enrolment.
Intune rules a device must meet; result used by Conditional Access.
Removes only corporate app data, leaving personal data intact.
Detection of mobile threats such as phishing and malicious apps, e.g. Defender for Endpoint.

lessons.trap: BYOD scenarios where users refuse enrolment point to app protection policies plus 'Require app protection policy', not device compliance.
lessons.example: Contractors' personal iPhones get Outlook with an app protection policy, and Conditional Access requires that policy before Exchange Online access.

lessons.title: IoT devices and embedded systems
lessons.short: IoT and embedded devices often cannot run agents, so requirements focus on unique device identity, secure provisioning, network isolation, firmware updates and agentless monitoring. Enterprise IoT such as printers and cameras is discovered by Defender for Endpoint and Defender for IoT.
lessons.deep:
Requirements for IoT devices and embedded systems:
- **Unique identity per device**: X.509 certificates (ideally backed by a hardware root of trust such as a TPM or secure element), never one shared key for a fleet. Use **Azure IoT Hub Device Provisioning Service (DPS)** for zero-touch, secure enrolment.
- **Least privilege and secure defaults**: no default passwords, disable unused services and ports.
- **Secure update**: signed firmware and an update mechanism (for example Device Update for IoT Hub).
- **Network segmentation**: place devices in isolated segments/VLANs, allow only required flows, no direct internet inbound.
- **Monitoring**: because many devices cannot host an agent, use **agentless, network-based** detection. **Enterprise IoT** in Microsoft Defender for IoT uses Defender for Endpoint network discovery to inventory printers, VoIP phones, smart TVs and cameras and show vulnerabilities and alerts in the Defender portal.
- **Device-side agent** for builders: the Defender for IoT **micro agent** is scheduled to retire on **1 June 2027**, so avoid basing new designs on it.

These map to the Zero Trust idea of explicitly verifying every device, not trusting the network.

terms.d: Azure service that securely enrols IoT devices into the right IoT hub at scale.
TPM or secure element that protects device keys and attests identity.
Defender for IoT capability that discovers IT-network IoT devices via Defender for Endpoint.

lessons.trap: Shared symmetric keys across a fleet are a classic wrong answer; per-device X.509 identity with DPS is the secure pattern.
lessons.example: A smart-building project issues each sensor its own X.509 certificate at the factory, enrols through DPS, and isolates sensors on a dedicated VLAN.

lessons.title: Securing OT and ICS with Defender for IoT
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for IoT protects operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) with agentless network sensors that receive mirrored traffic from a SPAN port or TAP and use deep packet inspection of industrial protocols. Sensors can be cloud-connected or fully air-gapped.
lessons.deep:
OT networks (PLCs, HMIs, SCADA, historians) cannot tolerate scanning or agents, so monitoring must be **passive**.

**OT network sensors** (physical appliance or VM) connect to a **SPAN (mirror) port or network TAP** and perform deep packet inspection of protocols such as Modbus, DNP3 and others. They build an asset inventory, a network map and vulnerability findings. Analysis happens **on the sensor**, so only metadata goes to Azure, which suits low-bandwidth sites.

**Analytics engines**: protocol violation, policy violation (deviation from a learned baseline), industrial malware (e.g. TRITON), anomaly and operational incidents.

**Deployment models**:
- **Cloud-connected**: alerts and inventory in the Azure portal or Defender portal, threat intelligence pushed automatically, integration with **Microsoft Sentinel** and Defender XDR.
- **Locally managed / air-gapped**: everything stays on the sensor console; threat intelligence is uploaded manually; integrate with on-premises SIEM.
- **Hybrid** of both.

The legacy **on-premises management console** is retired (not downloadable after 1 January 2025). Map detections to **MITRE ATT&CK for ICS** and align sensor placement to the network architecture (often the Purdue model).

terms.d: Switch port that mirrors traffic to a monitoring device.
Hardware device that copies traffic passively from a link.
Locally managed sensor with no cloud connection; data stays on-premises.
Knowledge base of adversary techniques against industrial control systems.

lessons.trap: OT answers must be passive and agentless; options that install agents on PLCs or run active vulnerability scans against OT are wrong.
lessons.example: A water utility with no internet at its treatment plant deploys locally managed sensors on SPAN ports and forwards alerts to its on-premises SIEM.

lessons.title: Security baselines for server and client endpoints
lessons.short: A security baseline is a Microsoft-recommended group of settings. Use Intune security baselines for managed Windows clients, Group Policy baselines from the Security Compliance Toolkit for domain-joined servers, and Azure Policy machine configuration to audit Azure and Arc servers against the MCSB compute baseline.
lessons.deep:
Baselines save you from designing hundreds of settings yourself. Pick the tool by how the device is managed:
- **Intune security baselines** (Endpoint security > Security baselines): Windows security baseline, **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** baseline, **Microsoft Edge**, **Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise**, **Windows 365** and others. Baselines are versioned: when a newer version ships, older profiles become read-only for settings, and you update a profile to the newer version. Baselines can conflict with other device configuration profiles, so check per-setting status.
- **Security Compliance Toolkit (SCT)**: Group Policy baseline packs plus **Policy Analyzer** (compare GPOs and find conflicts) and **LGPO** (apply to a standalone machine). Suits AD DS-joined servers.
- **Azure Policy machine configuration**: audits (and can configure) OS settings in Azure VMs and **Arc-enabled servers** against the Windows and Linux **Azure compute security baseline**; findings surface as Defender for Cloud recommendations (OS configuration assessment in Defender for Servers Plan 2).
- **Defender for Endpoint security settings management** can push some endpoint security policies from Intune to devices not enrolled in Intune.

Start in audit, test in a pilot ring, then enforce.

terms.d: Pre-configured group of recommended security settings from Microsoft.
SCT tool that compares GPO sets and highlights conflicts or redundancy.
MCSB-aligned OS settings audited by machine configuration.

lessons.trap: Intune baselines apply to Intune-managed devices; for domain-joined servers not in Intune, use Group Policy (SCT) or machine configuration through Arc.
lessons.example: Windows 11 laptops get the Intune Windows and Defender for Endpoint baselines, while Arc-enabled file servers are audited with machine configuration.

lessons.title: Windows LAPS
lessons.short: Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) is built into Windows. It rotates a local administrator password per device and backs it up to either Microsoft Entra ID or Active Directory, stopping attackers reusing one shared local password for lateral movement.
lessons.deep:
If every machine shares the same local admin password, one stolen hash unlocks the estate (pass-the-hash lateral movement). **Windows LAPS** gives each device a unique, rotating password.

Key facts:
- **Built in** to supported Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2019/2022/2025 (April 2023 update or later); the legacy Microsoft LAPS MSI is deprecated.
- **Backup target**: Entra-joined devices back up to **Microsoft Entra ID**; AD-joined to **Windows Server AD**; hybrid-joined devices pick **one** (not both). Entra backup needs only Entra ID Free; you must enable LAPS in Entra device settings.
- **Configuration**: Intune (LAPS CSP) for Entra and hybrid devices, Group Policy for AD-joined devices.
- **AD features**: password **encryption** (needs Windows Server 2016 domain functional level; encrypted to a principal, Domain Admins by default), **encrypted password history**, and backup of the **DSRM** password on domain controllers (AD only).
- **Post-authentication actions**: after the managed account is used, rotate the password (optionally sign out or reboot) after a grace period.
- **Read access**: in Entra, Global Administrator, Cloud Device Administrator and Intune Administrator can read passwords by default; use custom roles for least privilege.
- **Legacy LAPS emulation mode** eases migration but stores passwords in clear text.

terms.d: Built-in Windows feature that rotates and backs up a local admin password per device.
Directory Services Restore Mode password on domain controllers; LAPS can back it up to AD.
Rotate password, and optionally sign out or reboot, after the managed account is used.
Mode honouring old LAPS GPOs; stores passwords in clear text.

lessons.trap: A hybrid-joined device cannot back up to both Entra ID and AD; and DSRM backup and password encryption apply only to the AD target.
lessons.example: Hybrid-joined laptops back up LAPS passwords to Entra ID so helpdesk can retrieve them in the Intune portal, while DCs back up DSRM passwords to AD with encryption.

lessons.title: Security baselines for SaaS, PaaS and IaaS
lessons.short: Baselines differ by service model because the shared responsibility split differs. For IaaS you harden the OS; for PaaS you configure the service using its MCSB security baseline and Azure Policy; for SaaS you configure tenant settings and track them with Secure Score and SaaS security posture management.
lessons.deep:
The **shared responsibility model** decides what your baseline must cover:
- **IaaS (VMs)**: you own the OS, middleware and network rules. Baseline = OS hardening (Azure compute security baseline via machine configuration, CIS), patching, EDR, NSGs, disk encryption.
- **PaaS (App Service, Azure SQL, Storage, Key Vault)**: Microsoft runs the OS. You configure the service. Microsoft publishes a **per-service security baseline** that applies MCSB controls (network isolation, identity, data protection, logging) to that service. Enforce it with **Azure Policy** initiatives (Audit, Deny, DeployIfNotExists, Modify) assigned at **management group** scope, ideally inside an **Azure landing zone**.
- **SaaS (Microsoft 365, Salesforce, ServiceNow)**: you configure identity, sharing and tenant settings. Measure with **Microsoft Secure Score** and **SaaS security posture management (SSPM)** in Defender for Cloud Apps: connect the app with an **app connector**, turn on security recommendations, and track the **SaaS Security initiative** in Exposure Management.

Across all three: identity is always yours. Microsoft Entra ID, Conditional Access and least privilege appear in every baseline.

terms.d: Split of security duties between cloud provider and customer by service model.
What a policy does on evaluation: Audit, Deny, DeployIfNotExists, Modify and others.
SaaS security posture management: configuration assessment of connected SaaS apps.

lessons.trap: Do not specify OS hardening for PaaS or SaaS; on PaaS the customer configures the service, not the underlying OS.
lessons.example: A landing zone assigns a Deny policy that blocks storage accounts with public network access, while Salesforce settings are tracked through SSPM recommendations.

lessons.title: Security requirements for IoT workloads
lessons.short: An IoT workload is the cloud side of IoT: IoT Hub, provisioning, data pipelines and apps. Secure it with per-device authentication, private endpoints, Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC for services, least-privilege access policies, and monitoring of device and hub activity.
lessons.deep:
Device hardening (objective 3.2) is only half the story. The IoT **workload** in Azure also needs requirements:
- **Identity and authentication**: devices authenticate with X.509 certificates or per-device keys; back-end services use **Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC** (for example IoT Hub data roles) instead of shared access policies. Disable local (SAS) authentication where possible.
- **Network**: use **private endpoints** for IoT Hub and DPS, restrict or disable public network access, and use IP filters only as a supplement.
- **Data protection**: TLS 1.2+ in transit; data at rest is encrypted by the platform.
- **Provisioning**: DPS enrolment groups with certificate chains, and a plan to **revoke** compromised devices by disabling them in the hub or DPS.
- **Updates**: signed over-the-air updates (Device Update for IoT Hub).
- **Monitoring**: Azure Monitor diagnostic logs from IoT Hub into Sentinel; Defender for Cloud recommendations for IoT Hub configuration.
- **Edge**: IoT Edge gateways isolate leaf devices and should themselves be hardened.

Think of it as a Zero Trust data pipeline from device to dashboard.

terms.d: Azure PaaS that brokers bidirectional messages between devices and the cloud.
Key-based IoT Hub permission; prefer Entra ID and RBAC for services.
Runtime that runs cloud workloads on a local gateway device.

lessons.trap: Back-end apps using the iothubowner shared key is the wrong answer; prefer managed identity with Entra ID RBAC.
lessons.example: An analytics function reads telemetry from IoT Hub by using its managed identity and an IoT Hub data reader role, over a private endpoint.

lessons.title: Security requirements for web workloads
lessons.short: Web workloads need edge protection (Azure Front Door or Application Gateway with Web Application Firewall, plus DDoS Protection), HTTPS-only with TLS 1.2+, managed identities and Key Vault references for secrets, private connectivity to back ends, and API protection with Azure API Management and Defender for APIs.
lessons.deep:
Layered requirements for a web app or API:
- **Edge**: **Azure Front Door Premium** (global) or **Application Gateway** (regional) with **Azure Web Application Firewall** using managed rule sets (OWASP-based Default Rule Set) and bot protection. Start WAF in **Detection** mode, tune, then switch to **Prevention**. Lock the origin so it accepts traffic only from the edge (for example Front Door Private Link to the origin, or access restrictions on the Front Door service tag plus header check).
- **DDoS**: Azure DDoS Protection (**Network Protection** per VNet, or **IP Protection** per public IP). Network Protection adds rapid response, cost protection and a WAF discount.
- **App Service settings**: **HTTPS Only** (not on by default), minimum TLS 1.2, disable FTP or require FTPS, disable basic auth for SCM/FTP, **Easy Auth** with Microsoft Entra ID.
- **Secrets**: **managed identity** plus **Key Vault references** in app settings.
- **Back ends**: **VNet integration** for outbound and **private endpoints** for databases and storage.
- **APIs**: **Azure API Management** for authentication (validate-jwt), rate limiting and versioning; **Defender for APIs** for inventory, sensitive data classification and OWASP API Top 10 threat detection.
- **Threat protection**: Defender for App Service; DevSecOps code scanning (GitHub Advanced Security).

terms.d: Web Application Firewall on Front Door or Application Gateway; modes Detection and Prevention.
App setting syntax that resolves a secret from Key Vault at runtime.
Plan protecting APIs published in Azure API Management.
App Service built-in authentication with Entra ID and other providers.

lessons.trap: Azure Firewall is not a WAF; HTTP-layer attacks such as SQL injection on a public site need Azure WAF on Front Door or Application Gateway.
lessons.example: A global e-commerce site uses Front Door Premium with WAF in Prevention mode, Private Link to App Service origins, and Key Vault references for its payment API keys.

lessons.title: Security requirements for containers
lessons.short: Container requirements cover the supply chain and runtime: build from trusted minimal base images, scan images in the registry, sign and only deploy approved images, keep secrets out of images, run as non-root, and detect runtime threats and binary drift with Defender for Containers.
lessons.deep:
Containers move risk into the **build pipeline**. Requirements:
- **Registry**: Azure Container Registry with private endpoints, public access disabled, Entra ID auth (admin user disabled), and RBAC such as AcrPull for clusters.
- **Image vulnerability assessment**: Defender for Containers (and Defender CSPM agentless assessment) scans images in ACR, ECR, GAR/GCR and supported external registries using **Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management**, and scans running containers.
- **Supply chain**: sign images (for example Notation with signatures stored in ACR) and only admit signed, scanned images; generate SBOMs; scan in CI (GitHub Advanced Security, Defender for Cloud DevOps security) so issues are fixed before push.
- **Image hygiene**: minimal/distroless base images, no secrets baked in (use Key Vault and workload identity), pin versions.
- **Runtime**: run as **non-root**, read-only root filesystem, drop Linux capabilities, no privileged containers.
- **Runtime threat detection**: the **Defender sensor** provides Kubernetes-aware detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for Containers, plus **binary drift detection** (alert on, or block, executables not in the original image).

Serverless containers (Azure Container Apps, ACI) still need image scanning and identity controls.

terms.d: A process running in a container that was not part of the original image.
Azure RBAC role allowing an identity to pull images from ACR.
Software bill of materials listing the components inside an image.

lessons.trap: Scanning only at build time misses newly published CVEs; the exam expects continuous registry and runtime scanning too.
lessons.example: A pipeline signs each image after scanning, and the cluster's admission policy rejects any unsigned image pulled from a public registry.

lessons.title: Security requirements for container orchestration (AKS)
lessons.short: For AKS, secure the control plane (Microsoft Entra integration, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes, local accounts disabled, private cluster or authorized IP ranges), the workloads (workload identity, Pod Security Admission, Azure Policy, network policies), and the nodes (upgrades and node image patching), with Defender for Containers on top.
lessons.deep:
**Control plane access**
- Integrate with **Microsoft Entra ID**, authorise with **Azure RBAC for Kubernetes** or Kubernetes RBAC bound to Entra groups, least privilege per namespace.
- **Disable local accounts** (`--disable-local-accounts`) so the static admin kubeconfig cannot be retrieved; rotate certificates if local accounts were used before.
- Keep the API server off the internet: **private cluster**, or **authorized IP ranges**.
- Use Conditional Access and PIM for cluster admin groups.

**Workloads**
- **Microsoft Entra Workload ID** (workload identity) gives pods federated identities without secrets.
- **Pod Security Admission** (baseline/restricted standards) and the **Azure Policy add-on for AKS** (Gatekeeper) to deny privileged pods, enforce allowed registries and resource limits.
- **Network policies** (Azure, Calico or Cilium) for east-west segmentation, including blocking pod access to the instance metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 where not needed.
- Egress through **Azure Firewall** with a user-defined route.
- Secrets from Key Vault through the **Secrets Store CSI driver**.

**Nodes and platform**: stay on supported Kubernetes versions, apply **node image upgrades** (nightly patches do not update the base image), and enable **Defender for Containers** for control-plane and runtime detections across AKS, EKS, GKE and Arc-enabled clusters.

terms.d: Uses Azure role assignments to authorise Kubernetes API actions.
Federated Entra identity for pods, replacing stored secrets.
Built-in Kubernetes controller enforcing Pod Security Standards per namespace.
AKS cluster whose API server has only a private IP.

lessons.trap: Entra integration alone still leaves the local admin kubeconfig usable; you must also disable local accounts.
lessons.example: A regulated AKS cluster is private, has local accounts disabled, uses workload identity for pods, and egresses through Azure Firewall.

lessons.title: Security solutions for Azure AI services
lessons.short: Secure Azure AI services and Microsoft Foundry like any PaaS, plus AI-specific controls: Microsoft Entra ID with local (key) authentication disabled, managed identities, private endpoints, customer-managed keys, Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields, Defender for AI Services threat protection and AI security posture management in Defender CSPM.
lessons.deep:
**Platform controls**
- **Identity**: use Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC, not API keys. Set **disableLocalAuth = true**, and enforce it with the built-in policy *Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled*. Note propagation can take minutes to hours, so verify with a 401 test.
- **Managed identities** for apps calling models and for the AI resource reaching storage and search.
- **Network**: private endpoints, public network access disabled, managed network isolation for Foundry hubs/projects.
- **Data**: encryption at rest with **customer-managed keys** in Key Vault where required; identity-based (not shared key) storage access.

**AI-specific controls**
- **Azure AI Content Safety** filters and **Prompt Shields** for jailbreak and indirect prompt injection.
- **Defender for AI Services** (Defender for Cloud): real-time alerts for jailbreak, data leakage, data poisoning, credential theft and more; works with Prompt Shields and threat intelligence; alerts flow to Defender XDR. Text tokens only; commercial clouds only.
- **AI security posture management** in **Defender CSPM**: discovers AI workloads, misconfigurations and attack paths to AI resources.
- **Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI** for prompts and sensitive data in AI interactions.

Align with MCSB v2 AI security domain.

terms.d: Resource property that turns off key-based access so only Entra ID tokens work.
Azure AI Content Safety feature detecting jailbreak and prompt injection attempts.
Defender for Cloud plan for runtime threat protection of generative AI apps.
AI security posture management in Defender CSPM.

lessons.trap: Regenerating API keys is not the same as disabling key access; the Zero Trust answer is disableLocalAuth plus Entra ID and managed identity.
lessons.example: A chatbot built in Foundry calls its model with a managed identity over a private endpoint, while Defender for AI Services alerts the SOC to jailbreak attempts.

lessons.title: Evaluating network designs against best practices
lessons.short: Assess a network design against Zero Trust and MCSB network security: hub-and-spoke or Virtual WAN with central Azure Firewall, segmentation with NSGs and application security groups, private endpoints instead of public PaaS access, DDoS Protection and WAF at the edge, and no direct internet management ports.
lessons.deep:
When you evaluate a design, check these areas:
