- **Topology**: **hub-and-spoke** (or **Azure Virtual WAN** secured hubs) with shared services in the hub, workloads in spokes, all in an **Azure landing zone**. Spokes are not peered to each other directly; traffic flows through the hub firewall.
- **Segmentation**: **network security groups (NSGs)** at subnet/NIC, **application security groups** to group VMs by role, default deny; micro-segmentation for sensitive tiers.
- **Inspection**: **Azure Firewall** with user-defined routes (0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall). Pick the SKU: **Basic** (up to 250 Mbps, small sites), **Standard** (threat intelligence filtering, web categories, DNS proxy), **Premium** (**TLS inspection**, signature-based **IDPS**, full-path **URL filtering**) for sensitive workloads. Manage rules centrally with **Azure Firewall Manager** policies.
- **PaaS access**: **Private Link/private endpoints** with private DNS zones; disable public network access. Service endpoints are a weaker, older option.
- **Edge**: **Azure DDoS Protection** and **Azure WAF** (Front Door or Application Gateway).
- **Admin access**: **Azure Bastion** or JIT; no public RDP/SSH.
- **Visibility**: VNet flow logs, Traffic Analytics, Firewall logs to Sentinel.
- **Hybrid**: ExpressRoute/VPN, and increasingly **SSE** (Global Secure Access) replacing legacy VPN for users.

terms.d: Topology with shared security services in a hub VNet and workloads in peered spokes.
Logical group of NICs used as source/destination in NSG rules.
SKU adding TLS inspection, signature IDPS and URL filtering.
Private IP in your VNet for a PaaS resource via Private Link.

lessons.trap: TLS inspection and IDPS are Premium-only; a stem requiring inspection of encrypted outbound traffic rules out Firewall Standard and Basic.
lessons.example: Reviewing a design, the architect replaces spoke-to-spoke peering with forced routing through a Premium firewall in the hub and moves SQL to private endpoints.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra Internet Access as a secure web gateway
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra Internet Access is the identity-aware secure web gateway (SWG) in Global Secure Access, Microsoft's Security Service Edge. The Global Secure Access client or remote networks forward internet traffic, and web content filtering policies in security profiles, linked through Conditional Access, allow or block by category, FQDN or URL.
lessons.deep:
**Security Service Edge (SSE)** moves network security to the cloud close to users. Microsoft's SSE is **Global Secure Access**, made up of **Microsoft Entra Internet Access** and **Microsoft Entra Private Access**.

**How Internet Access works**
- Traffic is acquired by the **Global Secure Access client** (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android) or from branches via **remote networks**, and sent to Microsoft's edge.
- Enable the **Internet Access traffic forwarding profile**.
- Build **web content filtering policies** (rules by **web category**, **FQDN** or URL, action Allow or Block).
- Group policies into a **security profile** with a priority.
- Link the profile in a **Conditional Access** policy targeting **All internet resources with Global Secure Access**, session control **Use Global Secure Access security profile**. This makes filtering **user- and context-aware**.
- The **baseline profile** applies to all Internet Access traffic, including remote networks, without Conditional Access.
- **TLS inspection** lets it see inside HTTPS for URL path rules; threat intelligence filtering, DLP and AI protections such as prompt injection protection extend it.

**Licensing**: Internet Access is in the **Microsoft Entra Suite** or sold standalone; users also need Entra ID P1/P2.

Compared with Azure Firewall: Firewall protects Azure workloads' egress; Internet Access protects **users** wherever they are.

terms.d: Cloud-delivered SWG, CASB and ZTNA services; Microsoft's is Global Secure Access.
Service that filters user web traffic by policy.
Prioritised group of web filtering policies, applied through Conditional Access.
Defines which traffic (Microsoft, Internet, Private) the client tunnels.

lessons.trap: A filtering policy does nothing per user until its security profile is linked through a Conditional Access session control (or placed in the baseline profile).
lessons.example: Finance users get a security profile that blocks gambling and file-sharing categories, applied through a Conditional Access policy scoped to the Finance group.

lessons.title: Internet Access for Microsoft services and cross-tenant control
lessons.short: The Microsoft traffic profile, included with Entra ID P1/P2, tunnels Microsoft 365 and Entra traffic through Global Secure Access. It enables universal tenant restrictions (enforcing tenant restrictions v2 without a proxy), the compliant network check in Conditional Access, and source IP restoration in sign-in logs.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft traffic profile** features:
- **Universal tenant restrictions**: enforces **tenant restrictions v2 (TRv2)** policies, configured in **cross-tenant access settings**, for all devices with the client or on a remote network, **without a corporate proxy injecting headers**. Users can sign in only to allowed tenants and apps, which stops data exfiltration to personal or foreign tenants. You must first configure the TRv2 default and partner policies, then enable it under Global Secure Access > Settings > Session management.
- **Compliant network check**: Conditional Access location condition **All Compliant Network locations**. It is tenant-specific and replaces brittle IP-based named locations. It is enforced at sign-in (stolen refresh tokens replayed elsewhere fail) and, for **CAE**-capable apps such as Microsoft Graph and Exchange Online, on the data plane in near real time.
- **Source IP restoration**: sign-in logs and risk detections see the user's real public IP rather than the SSE egress IP.

**Cross-tenant design**: TRv2 restricts **your users** going to **other** tenants (outbound control at your network). **Cross-tenant access settings** inbound/outbound govern B2B collaboration and direct connect. For external users who need your private apps, Global Secure Access supports **B2B guest access**: the guest signs in with their home account and switches to the resource tenant in the client; the resource tenant's policies apply and the home tenant needs no GSA licence.

terms.d: Policy limiting which external tenants your users can access from your devices/network.
Global Secure Access enforcement of TRv2 without a header-injecting proxy.
Conditional Access condition met only when traffic comes through your tenant's GSA.
Preserves the user's original IP in Entra logs when tunnelled via GSA.

lessons.trap: Blocking access to other organisations' tenants from corporate devices is tenant restrictions (TRv2 via universal tenant restrictions), not inbound cross-tenant access settings, which control guests coming into your tenant.
lessons.example: To stop staff uploading data to personal OneDrive or a competitor's tenant, Contoso configures TRv2 to allow only its own and a partner tenant and enables universal tenant restrictions.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra Private Access
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra Private Access is Microsoft's zero trust network access (ZTNA). It replaces VPNs by giving users access to specific private apps, defined by FQDN, IP and port, through Global Secure Access, with Conditional Access per app and outbound-only private network connectors in the datacenter.
lessons.deep:
Traditional VPNs put a user **on the network**, enabling lateral movement. **Private Access** grants access **per application**.

**Components**
- **Global Secure Access client** with the **Private Access traffic forwarding profile**.
- **Microsoft Entra private network connectors** (the evolution of application proxy connectors) installed on servers near the apps. They make **outbound-only** connections, so no inbound firewall ports are needed. Group them into **connector groups** per site.
- Apps defined as **enterprise applications**:
  - **Quick Access**: one broad app containing FQDNs, IP ranges and ports, the fast path to replace VPN.
  - **Global Secure Access (per-app) applications**: separate apps for subsets that need their own users, Conditional Access policies or time limits.

**Security**: assign users/groups per app; apply **Conditional Access** per app (MFA, compliant device, authentication strength, even for legacy protocols such as RDP, SMB or SSH). Supports TCP and UDP, **private DNS** for internal names, and SSO, including Kerberos to on-premises apps. Integrates with Entra ID Protection and CAE.

**Licensing**: in the **Microsoft Entra Suite** or standalone (plus Entra ID P1/P2). Design pattern: start with Quick Access to retire VPN, then carve high-value apps into per-app applications with stricter policies.

terms.d: Zero trust network access: per-app access instead of network-level VPN access.
Outbound-only agent that brokers Private Access traffic to internal apps.
Single Private Access app covering broad FQDN/IP ranges to replace VPN.
Separate Private Access apps with their own assignments and CA policies.

lessons.trap: If a subset of private resources needs stricter Conditional Access than the rest, move it from Quick Access into its own per-app Global Secure Access application.
lessons.example: Engineers reach a legacy SSH jump host through a per-app Private Access application that requires phishing-resistant MFA, while general file shares stay in Quick Access.

lessons.title: Measuring M365 posture with Secure Score
lessons.short: Microsoft Secure Score, in the Microsoft Defender portal, measures the security posture of identity, devices, email, collaboration and connected SaaS apps. It awards points for completed recommended actions and tracks history, so you can compare against similar organisations and set KPIs.
lessons.deep:
An architect needs a number to report progress. For Microsoft 365, that number is **Microsoft Secure Score** (security.microsoft.com/securescore).

How it works:
- Recommendations cover products such as Microsoft Entra ID, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps and some connected SaaS apps.
- Each **recommended action** is worth up to 10 points. Most are all-or-nothing. Some give **partial points**: if 50 of 100 users have MFA on a 10-point action, you earn 5.
- You can set a status on each action: **Planned**, **Risk accepted**, or **Resolved through alternative mitigation** when a non-Microsoft tool already covers it. Alternative mitigation still earns points.
- **History**, **metrics and trends**, and **comparison** with similar organisations let you show improvement over time.

Access comes from Entra roles (Security Reader to view, Security Administrator to manage) or Defender Unified RBAC with Exposure Management permissions.

Don't mix it up with the **Defender for Cloud secure score**, which measures Azure and multicloud resources against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark.

terms.d: Defender portal measurement of Microsoft 365 and connected app posture, based on recommended actions.
A single hardening step worth up to 10 points, sometimes with partial credit.
Status for an action covered by a non-Microsoft tool or other control; it still earns points.
Status recording a decision not to implement an action. It earns no points.

lessons.trap: Exam options swap Microsoft Secure Score (Microsoft 365) with the Defender for Cloud secure score (Azure resources) or the Compliance Manager compliance score (regulations).
lessons.example: The CISO wants a quarterly board metric for M365 hardening. You track Microsoft Secure Score history, compare it with organisations of similar size, and mark MFA from a third-party IdP as alternative mitigation.

lessons.title: Evaluating Defender for Office 365
lessons.short: Exchange Online Protection (EOP) blocks bulk, known email threats for every cloud mailbox. Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 adds Safe Links, Safe Attachments and impersonation protection. Plan 2 adds Threat Explorer, AIR, attack simulation training and Campaigns.
lessons.deep:
Email and collaboration are the top entry points for phishing and ransomware, so an architect must know what each layer adds.

**EOP** comes with every Microsoft 365 subscription that has cloud mailboxes. It provides anti-malware, anti-spam, spoof intelligence, connection filtering, quarantine, the Tenant Allow/Block List and **zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)** for email.

**Defender for Office 365 Plan 1** targets zero-day malware, phishing and business email compromise (BEC):
- **Safe Attachments**: detonates attachments in a sandbox. It also covers files in SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams.
- **Safe Links**: time-of-click URL checks in email, Office apps and Teams.
- **Anti-phishing extras**: user and domain **impersonation protection** and mailbox intelligence.
- **Real-time detections**, ZAP for Teams and priority account tags.

**Plan 2** adds the post-breach and SOC tools: **Threat Explorer**, **Threat Trackers**, **Campaigns**, **Automated Investigation and Response (AIR)**, **attack simulation training**, priority account protection, and advanced hunting and incidents in Microsoft Defender XDR.

Plan 2 is included in Microsoft 365 E5. The quick way to tell which plan you have: the portal shows Real-time detections for Plan 1 and Explorer for Plan 2.

terms.d: Built-in filtering for all cloud mailboxes: anti-malware, anti-spam, spoof protection, ZAP.
Sandbox detonation of attachments and files (Plan 1).
Time-of-click URL rewriting and checking (Plan 1).
Automated Investigation and Response playbooks for email threats (Plan 2).

lessons.trap: Threat Explorer, AIR and attack simulation training need Plan 2. Safe Links, Safe Attachments and impersonation protection are already in Plan 1.
lessons.example: A firm on Microsoft 365 E3 keeps getting CEO-impersonation emails. Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 adds impersonation protection and Safe Links without paying for the Plan 2 SOC tooling.

lessons.title: Evaluating Defender for Cloud Apps
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is Microsoft's CASB. It discovers shadow IT (Cloud Discovery), connects to SaaS apps through APIs (app connectors), controls browser sessions in real time (Conditional Access app control), and governs OAuth apps (app governance). It also covers SaaS posture (SSPM).
lessons.deep:
A **cloud access security broker (CASB)** sits between users and cloud apps. **Defender for Cloud Apps** offers several controls, and the exam expects you to pick the right one:

- **Cloud Discovery**: analyses traffic logs (log upload, log collector, or the **Defender for Endpoint** integration) and rates apps against 90+ risk factors from the **cloud app catalog**. Apps you mark **Unsanctioned** can be blocked on devices onboarded to Defender for Endpoint.
- **App connectors**: API connections to apps such as Microsoft 365, Salesforce or Box. They let file and activity policies scan data at rest, apply labels and remove external sharing. This is near-real-time, not inline.
- **Conditional Access app control**: an Entra Conditional Access policy with the session control **Use Conditional Access App Control** sends browser sessions through a reverse proxy. **Session policies** can then block download, cut, copy or print, or **protect on download** with a Purview sensitivity label. It doesn't work for desktop clients such as the Teams desktop app.
- **App governance**: finds overprivileged, unused or malicious **OAuth apps**.
- **SSPM**: finds SaaS misconfigurations and feeds them into Secure Score.

Alerts are correlated into incidents in Microsoft Defender XDR.

terms.d: Shadow IT discovery from traffic logs or Defender for Endpoint, with app risk scores.
API integration with a SaaS app that gives visibility and governance of data at rest.
Reverse proxy that enforces real-time session policies in browser sessions.
Monitors and governs OAuth app permissions and behaviour.

lessons.trap: For real-time blocking of downloads on unmanaged devices, the answer is a session policy through Conditional Access app control, not an app connector file policy, which acts after the fact.
lessons.example: Contractors on personal laptops may view Salesforce reports but not download them. A CA policy routes their browser sessions to Defender for Cloud Apps, and a session policy blocks downloads.

lessons.title: Device management with Microsoft Intune
lessons.short: Microsoft Intune manages devices (MDM) and apps (MAM). Compliance policies feed Conditional Access ('Require device to be marked as compliant'). App protection policies protect corporate data in apps on unenrolled BYOD devices ('Require app protection policy'). Defender for Endpoint risk can be part of compliance.
lessons.deep:
In Zero Trust, device health is a signal for every access decision. **Microsoft Intune** supplies that signal.

- **Enrolment (MDM)**: corporate devices enrol, often through **Windows Autopilot**. Intune then deploys **configuration profiles** (settings), **endpoint security policies** (antivirus, disk encryption, firewall, EDR onboarding) and apps.
- **Compliance policies** define what healthy means: OS version, BitLocker, a password, and optionally **'Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score'** from **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint**. Entra Conditional Access then uses the grant control **Require device to be marked as compliant**.
- **App protection policies (MAM)** work **without enrolment**. They apply to managed apps such as Outlook and Teams on iOS/iPadOS, Android and Windows. They can encrypt corporate data, restrict cut/copy/paste and save-as, require a PIN, and allow **selective wipe** of corporate data only. Conditional Access pairs them with **Require app protection policy**.

When evaluating: corporate-owned devices need enrolment plus compliance. BYOD where users refuse enrolment needs MAM plus app protection. Intune Plan 1 is included in Microsoft 365 E3 and E5.

terms.d: Intune rules that mark a device compliant or not; consumed by Conditional Access.
App-level data protection that works on enrolled or unenrolled devices.
Removes only corporate data from managed apps, leaving personal data.
Defender for Endpoint risk level that a compliance policy can require.

lessons.trap: For BYOD devices that can't be enrolled, the exam wants app protection policies plus 'Require app protection policy', not compliance policies, which need enrolment.
lessons.example: A hospital lets clinicians use their own phones for Teams. MAM-without-enrolment encrypts Teams data, blocks copy to personal apps, and supports selective wipe when someone leaves.

lessons.title: Securing M365 data with Microsoft Purview
lessons.short: Microsoft Purview protects Microsoft 365 data with sensitivity labels (classify, encrypt, mark), DLP (stop risky sharing), retention (keep or delete), Insider Risk Management, eDiscovery and Audit. Container labels secure Teams, groups and sites. Auto-labelling can run in Office apps (client-side) or in the service (data at rest).
lessons.deep:
Evaluating Microsoft 365 data security means matching Purview solutions to risks:

- **Sensitivity labels** classify items and can apply **encryption** (usage rights such as VIEW, EDIT, EXTRACT), headers and watermarks. Protection travels with the file.
- **Container labels** apply to **Teams, Microsoft 365 groups and SharePoint sites**. They control privacy, guest access, external sharing and unmanaged-device access. They do **not** label the files inside.
- **Auto-labelling**: **client-side** in Office apps (recommend or apply while users work), and **service-side** auto-labelling policies for files at rest in SharePoint/OneDrive and email in transit. Service-side policies run in **simulation** first.
- **DLP** policies detect sensitive information types (SITs) or labels across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, endpoints and more, then warn, block or audit.
- **Retention policies and labels** (Data Lifecycle and Records Management) keep or delete content.
- **Insider Risk Management** and **Adaptive Protection** spot risky users and tighten DLP for them automatically.
- **Audit**: Audit (Standard) keeps records for 180 days by default. Audit (Premium) keeps them for one year by default, with longer add-ons.

terms.d: Classification tag that can encrypt, mark, and drive DLP or Copilot behaviour.
Label scoped to Teams, groups and sites that controls privacy and sharing.
Policy that labels data at rest in SharePoint/OneDrive and mail in transit.
Uses insider risk levels to apply stricter DLP to high-risk users.

lessons.trap: A label on a Team or site does not label the documents inside it. To classify existing files you need default library labels or auto-labelling.
lessons.example: M&A projects live in private Teams. A container label blocks guests and unmanaged-device downloads, and a service-side auto-labelling policy applies 'Highly Confidential' to files containing deal codes.

lessons.title: Data security for Microsoft 365 Copilot
lessons.short: Microsoft 365 Copilot only uses data the user can already access, so oversharing is the main risk. Use DSPM oversharing assessments, SharePoint Advanced Management (Restricted Content Discovery, access reviews), sensitivity labels, and a DLP policy for the Microsoft 365 Copilot location. Then audit, retain and eDiscover Copilot interactions.
lessons.deep:
Copilot grounds answers in Microsoft Graph content through the user's own permissions. It respects labels: for encrypted items, the user needs the **EXTRACT** and **VIEW** usage rights. Generated content inherits the **highest-priority label** of its sources where supported. The risk is that Copilot can surface content that was overshared.

Controls an architect layers:
- **DSPM** in Microsoft Purview (the unified experience; the classic DSPM for AI view is being retired) runs **data risk assessments** for oversharing and offers one-click policies.
- **SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM)** features come with Copilot licences. **Restricted Content Discovery** hides chosen sites from Copilot and org-wide search without changing permissions. Others include **restricted access control**, site access reviews and permission-state reports.
- A **DLP policy for the Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Chat location** (Custom template only, in its own policy) can stop Copilot processing **labelled items**, or block prompts containing **SITs**. Labels and SITs need separate rules. Changes can take up to four hours.
- **Audit**, **eDiscovery**, **retention**, **Communication Compliance** and Insider Risk's **Risky AI usage** template cover prompts and responses.

terms.d: SAM setting that hides a site from Copilot and org-wide search; permissions stay the same.
DLP location that stops Copilot processing labelled items or prompts that contain SITs.
Rights Management permission Copilot needs, along with VIEW, to use encrypted content.
Purview Data Security Posture Management, including AI oversharing assessments.

lessons.trap: Copilot never grants new access. The fix for 'Copilot shows salary files' is to fix oversharing (permissions, RCD, labels and DLP), not to block Copilot licences.
lessons.example: Before rollout, a DSPM assessment finds 40 sites shared with 'Everyone except external users'. You apply Restricted Content Discovery while owners run site access reviews.

lessons.title: Evaluating application portfolio posture
lessons.short: Start with inventory: which apps exist, where they run, who owns them, how exposed they are and how sensitive their data is. Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Defender CSPM, DevOps security connectors) gives posture findings from code to runtime. Rank fixes by business criticality and exposure.
lessons.deep:
Before redesigning, you assess what exists. A sound **application portfolio assessment**:

1. **Inventory** every app with an owner, hosting model (IaaS, App Service, AKS, Functions, SaaS), data classification and internet exposure.
2. **Score business criticality**: what happens if it is down, leaks or is tampered with.
3. **Gather posture data**:
   - **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** recommendations for App Service, containers, APIs and databases, measured against the **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)**.
   - **DevOps security** connectors for **Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab** surface code, secret, dependency and IaC findings.
   - **Defender CSPM** adds **attack path analysis**, **Cloud Security Explorer** and code-to-cloud context, for example an internet-exposed VM that can reach a sensitive storage account.
   - **Defender for Cloud Apps** for SaaS apps and OAuth apps.
4. **Prioritise**: internet-facing plus sensitive data plus exploitable findings come first.

The output is a ranked remediation backlog and a target architecture, often aligned to the **Well-Architected Framework** security pillar.

terms.d: Paid Defender for Cloud posture plan with attack paths, Cloud Security Explorer and code-to-cloud context.
Defender for Cloud connectors that bring in Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab findings.
Shows exploitable chains from exposure to critical assets.
How much damage loss of an app's confidentiality, integrity or availability would cause.

lessons.trap: Microsoft Secure Score measures Microsoft 365 posture. For Azure-hosted app portfolios, the exam wants Defender for Cloud and Defender CSPM.
lessons.example: A bank's 180 apps are mapped in Defender for Cloud. Attack paths show three internet-facing App Services with managed identities that can reach PII storage, and those go to the top of the backlog.

lessons.title: Threat modeling business-critical apps
lessons.short: Threat modeling finds design flaws before attackers do. Draw a data flow diagram with trust boundaries, then use STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) to list threats and pick mitigations. The Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool automates this.
lessons.deep:
**Threat modeling** is a structured design review, and it is one of the core practices of the Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL). Microsoft describes five steps: **define security requirements, create an application diagram, identify threats, mitigate threats, validate mitigations**.

The diagram is a **data flow diagram (DFD)**: processes, data stores, external entities, data flows and **trust boundaries** (where privilege or ownership changes, such as internet to web tier). Threats cluster at boundary crossings.

**STRIDE** maps each threat to the security property it breaks:
- **S**poofing → authentication (MFA, managed identities)
- **T**ampering → integrity (signing, hashing, TLS)
- **R**epudiation → non-repudiation (audit logs, ledger)
- **I**nformation disclosure → confidentiality (encryption, access control)
- **D**enial of service → availability (DDoS Protection, rate limits, WAF)
- **E**levation of privilege → authorisation (least privilege, RBAC)

The free **Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool** generates candidate threats from the DFD. Threat models should be revisited whenever the architecture changes. For business-critical apps, also weigh likelihood and impact (for example with DREAD-style scoring or CVSS) to rank mitigations.

terms.d: Threat categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege.
Point in a DFD where data crosses between different privilege levels or owners.
Model of processes, stores, entities and flows used to find threats.
Free Microsoft tool that suggests STRIDE threats from a DFD.

lessons.trap: Repudiation is mitigated by logging and audit trails, not encryption. The exam often pairs STRIDE categories with the wrong control.
lessons.example: Modelling a payments API shows that the API-to-database flow crosses a trust boundary with no auditing. You add Azure SQL auditing and ledger tables to address repudiation and tampering.

lessons.title: Full-lifecycle application security strategy
lessons.short: A full-lifecycle (DevSecOps) strategy builds security into every phase: plan, code, build, test, release, operate. Shift left with threat modeling, secret scanning, SAST and dependency scanning. Gate releases with IaC and container scanning. Keep protecting at runtime with Defender for Cloud, WAF and monitoring.
lessons.deep:
Application security is not a single pen test before go-live. A **full-lifecycle strategy** puts controls into each stage:

- **Plan/design**: security requirements, threat modeling, security champions.
- **Code**: secure coding standards, IDE linters, **secret scanning with push protection** (stops secrets before they reach the repo).
- **Commit/PR**: **SAST** (for example CodeQL code scanning) and **software composition analysis (SCA)** for vulnerable open-source dependencies. Branch protection requires review.
- **Build**: **IaC scanning** (Bicep, Terraform, ARM), **container image scanning**, signed artefacts and an SBOM. Pull dependencies from trusted feeds.
- **Test**: **DAST** against the running app, and fuzzing for critical parsers.
- **Release**: Azure Policy guardrails, approvals and environment protection.
- **Operate**: Defender for Cloud workload protections, WAF, Microsoft Sentinel monitoring, vulnerability management and incident response feeding lessons back into design.

**Shift left** means finding issues early, where fixing them is cheapest. You still need runtime protection (**shield right**). Microsoft Defender for Cloud **DevOps security** gives one view across Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab pipelines.

terms.d: Static analysis of source code for vulnerabilities without running the app.
Dynamic testing of a running application from the outside.
Software composition analysis that finds vulnerable or risky open-source packages.
Moving security checks earlier in the development lifecycle.

lessons.trap: DAST needs a running app. Scanning source code is SAST. The exam also tests that shift left does not replace runtime protection.
lessons.example: A retailer adds push protection, CodeQL on PRs, Trivy-style image scanning in the build and DAST in staging. Defender for Cloud connects the findings to the production containers they affect.

lessons.title: Standards and practices for secure development
lessons.short: Secure development standards tell developers exactly what 'secure' means: the Microsoft SDL practices, OWASP Top 10 awareness, OWASP ASVS as testable requirements, and OWASP SAMM to measure programme maturity. Make them enforceable through templates, pipeline gates and training.
lessons.deep:
Standards turn good intentions into checkable rules. Useful references:

- **Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL)**: practices such as training, security requirements, threat modeling, approved tools and cryptography, managing open-source risk, security testing and incident response planning.
- **OWASP Top 10**: an awareness list of the most critical web app risks (broken access control, injection and others). **OWASP API Security Top 10** covers APIs.
- **OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)**: detailed, testable requirements at three levels. Good for acceptance criteria.
- **OWASP SAMM**: a maturity model for assessing and improving the whole software security programme.

Typical mandatory practices:
- No secrets in code. Use **Azure Key Vault** with **managed identities**.
- Parameterised queries and output encoding against injection and XSS.
- Entra ID for authentication through the Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL). Never write your own crypto.
- TLS 1.2+ everywhere, and current algorithms only.
- Peer review, branch protection, signed commits, and **secret scanning with push protection** (GitHub Secret Protection, or GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps).

Enforce through golden templates, policy-as-code and pipeline gates, not documents alone.

terms.d: Microsoft's set of security practices across the development lifecycle.
Testable verification requirements for application security at three levels.
Software Assurance Maturity Model for assessing programme maturity.
Secret scanning that blocks a push containing detected secrets.

lessons.trap: OWASP Top 10 is an awareness list, ASVS is the testable requirements standard, and SAMM measures maturity. Exam options swap them.
lessons.example: An insurer adopts ASVS Level 2 as the definition of done for customer-facing apps and turns on push protection. It measures yearly progress with SAMM.

lessons.title: Mapping technologies to app security requirements
lessons.short: Turn each requirement into a specific Microsoft control: identity (Entra ID, External ID, managed identities), secrets (Key Vault), edge protection (WAF, DDoS Protection), APIs (API Management, Defender for APIs), network isolation (Private Link), monitoring (Defender for Cloud, Sentinel) and data protection (encryption, Purview).
lessons.deep:
Architect questions often give a list of requirements and ask which service meets each one. Common mappings:

- **Workforce sign-in, MFA, Conditional Access**: Microsoft Entra ID.
- **Customer or partner sign-in**: **Microsoft Entra External ID** (external tenant for consumer apps, B2B collaboration for partners).
- **App-to-Azure authentication with no secrets**: **managed identities** or workload identity federation.
- **Secrets, keys, certificates and rotation**: **Azure Key Vault** (or Managed HSM).
- **OWASP Top 10 protection at L7**: **Azure WAF** on Application Gateway or Front Door.
- **Volumetric L3/L4 DDoS**: **Azure DDoS Protection**.
- **API throttling, token validation, versioning**: **Azure API Management**. API threat detection: **Defender for APIs**.
- **Private connectivity to PaaS**: **Private Link / private endpoints**.
- **Runtime threat detection**: **Defender for Cloud** workload plans (App Service, Containers, Servers, Databases, Storage, AI Services).
- **Code and pipeline security**: DevOps security plus GitHub Advanced Security.
- **SIEM/SOAR**: **Microsoft Sentinel**.

Also confirm the SKU or tier gives the needed feature (for example, Front Door Premium for managed WAF rules).

terms.d: Microsoft's CIAM and B2B platform for customers and partners.
Mitigation of network-layer volumetric attacks for public IPs.
Private IP in your VNet for a PaaS resource, through Azure Private Link.
Defender for Cloud plan for APIs published in Azure API Management.

lessons.trap: WAF and DDoS Protection are complementary: WAF handles L7 application attacks, and DDoS Protection handles L3/L4 floods. Picking just one is the common wrong answer.
lessons.example: A new citizen portal needs consumer sign-in, OWASP protection and secret-free database access. You map these to Entra External ID, Front Door Premium WAF and a managed identity to Azure SQL.

lessons.title: Designing workload identities
lessons.short: Workloads should authenticate to Azure without stored secrets. Use managed identities for Azure-hosted code (system-assigned tied to one resource, user-assigned shareable). Use workload identity federation for GitHub Actions, Kubernetes and other clouds. Conditional Access for workload identities can block risky service principals.
lessons.deep:
A **workload identity** is an identity for software: an app, service, pipeline or agent. Entra ID has three main types: **app registrations/service principals**, **managed identities** and (for AI agents) **Microsoft Entra Agent ID**.

Design rules:
- **Managed identities** for code running in Azure. **System-assigned**: created with the resource and deleted with it, 1:1. **User-assigned**: a standalone resource you can attach to many resources, with a lifecycle you control. That is useful for pre-granting RBAC, scale sets, and CMK at storage account creation.
- **Workload identity federation**: a **federated identity credential** on an app registration or user-assigned managed identity trusts tokens from an external IdP (GitHub Actions, AKS workload identity, Google Cloud, AWS, SPIFFE). The **issuer, subject and audience** must match exactly (case-sensitive, no wildcards). The limit is **20 per app or identity**.
- If you must use a service principal credential, prefer **certificates** over client secrets, stored in Key Vault and rotated.
- Least-privilege **Azure RBAC** at the narrowest scope.
- **Conditional Access for workload identities** (needs **Workload Identities Premium**) blocks single-tenant service principals by location or **service principal risk**. It doesn't apply to managed identities.

terms.d: Standalone identity resource that can be shared by multiple Azure resources.
Trust from an external OIDC issuer, matched on issuer, subject and audience.
Licence for Conditional Access, ID Protection and access reviews for workload identities.
Entra identity capability for AI agents.

lessons.trap: Conditional Access for workload identities can't target managed identities, and its only grant control is Block. Exams offer 'require MFA for the service principal' as a distractor.
lessons.example: GitHub Actions deploys Bicep to production. A federated credential with subject repo:contoso/app:environment:prod replaces the stored client secret, and only that environment can get a token.

lessons.title: Designing API Management security
lessons.short: Azure API Management (APIM) is the policy gateway in front of APIs. Validate OAuth tokens (validate-jwt or validate-azure-ad-token), throttle with rate-limit-by-key and quota-by-key, use managed identity to the back end, and place APIM in a VNet behind a WAF. Defender for APIs adds threat detection.
lessons.deep:
APIs expose business logic directly, and the **OWASP API Security Top 10** (broken object-level authorisation, broken authentication, unrestricted resource consumption and others) shows how they fail. **Azure API Management** centralises the controls:

- **Authentication**: subscription keys identify a caller but are **not strong authentication**. Validate OAuth 2.0 tokens with **validate-jwt** (any OpenID provider) or **validate-azure-ad-token** (Entra). Use **validate-client-certificate** for mTLS.
- **Abuse protection**: **rate-limit-by-key** (short sliding window, max 300 seconds) and **quota-by-key** (longer-term volume). Add **ip-filter**, validate-content and request size limits.
- **Back-end trust**: **authentication-managed-identity** gets an Entra token for the back end, so no credentials are stored. Lock the back end to accept traffic only from APIM.
- **Network**: deploy APIM in a VNet (**internal mode**) with **Application Gateway WAF** in front for public exposure. Use private endpoints to back ends.
- **Secrets**: named values backed by **Key Vault**.
- **Visibility**: **Defender for APIs** (for APIs published in APIM) gives inventory, unauthenticated and unused endpoint findings, data classification and runtime anomaly alerts. Logs go to Sentinel.

terms.d: APIM inbound policy that checks a JWT's signature, audience, issuer and claims.
APIM policy that throttles calls per key (for example IP or subscription) in a short window.
APIM gateway reachable only inside the VNet, usually fronted by Application Gateway.
List of the most critical API security risks.

lessons.trap: Exam options treat APIM subscription keys as authentication. For user or app identity, validate an OAuth token.
lessons.example: A partner API sits behind Application Gateway WAF, then APIM in internal mode. APIM validates Entra tokens, limits each partner to 100 calls a minute, and calls the back end with its managed identity.

lessons.title: Designing apps with Azure Web Application Firewall
lessons.short: Azure WAF protects web apps from L7 attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. Deploy it on Azure Front Door (global edge) or Application Gateway (regional). Use the Default Rule Set (DRS 2.2, anomaly scoring), Bot Manager, and custom rules for rate limiting and geo-filtering. Start in Detection mode, then switch to Prevention.
lessons.deep:
**Azure Web Application Firewall** runs as a **WAF policy** attached to one of these:
- **Azure Front Door**: global, at Microsoft's edge, so attacks are stopped close to the source. It suits multi-region and internet-scale apps. **Front Door Standard** supports only **custom rules**. **Front Door Premium** adds the **Microsoft-managed rule set**, **bot protection** and **Private Link to origins**.
- **Application Gateway WAF v2**: regional, inside your VNet. It suits single-region apps and internal apps, or fronting API Management in internal mode. Policies can be global, **per site (listener)** or **per URI**.

**Managed rules**: the **Default Rule Set (DRS) 2.2**, the newest and recommended version, is based on OWASP CRS 3.3.4 plus Microsoft Threat Intelligence rules. DRS 2.x uses **anomaly scoring**: Critical = 5, Error = 4, Warning = 3, Notice = 2. A request with a score of 5 or more triggers the action. **Bot Manager 1.1** classifies good, bad and unknown bots.

**Custom rules** handle geo-filtering, IP allow/deny and **rate limiting**.

**Modes**: **Detection** logs only. **Prevention** blocks. Roll out in Detection, tune false positives with **exclusions**, then move to Prevention. WAF complements **DDoS Protection**; it doesn't replace it.

terms.d: Resource holding managed and custom rules, attached to Front Door or Application Gateway.
Microsoft-managed WAF rule set; DRS 2.2 is the latest.
Matched rules add severity points; the action fires at a threshold of 5.
Removes a specific request attribute from rule evaluation to fix false positives.

lessons.trap: Managed rule sets and bot protection on Front Door need the Premium tier. Front Door Standard only supports custom WAF rules.
lessons.example: A global e-commerce site uses Front Door Premium WAF with DRS 2.2, Bot Manager and a rate-limit rule on /login. Two weeks in Detection mode tune out false positives before blocking is turned on.

lessons.title: Data discovery and classification solutions
lessons.short: You can't protect data you can't find. Microsoft Purview classifies with sensitive information types, exact data match and trainable classifiers. The Purview Data Map scans Azure, on-premises and multicloud data stores. Defender for Cloud's sensitive data discovery samples cloud stores to prioritise security risk.
lessons.deep:
Discovery tools work at different depths, and choosing between them is a common architect decision.

**Classification methods** (shared across Purview):
- **Sensitive information types (SITs)**: patterns plus checksums and keywords, such as credit card numbers. Keyword dictionaries are a SIT variant.
- **Exact data match (EDM)**: matches actual values from your own database, such as real customer IDs, which gives few false positives.
- **Trainable classifiers**: machine-learning models for content without a pattern (contracts, résumés, source code).

**Where they run:**
- **Microsoft Purview Information Protection**: M365 content, with content explorer and auto-labelling.
- **Purview Data Map / Unified Catalog**: scans Azure SQL, Azure Storage/ADLS, Synapse, Cosmos DB, on-premises SQL Server, Amazon S3 and others, and applies classifications to a catalogue.
- **Defender for Cloud sensitive data discovery** (Defender CSPM and Defender for Storage): **smart sampling** of storage and databases to flag sensitive resources. Results feed **attack paths** and alert priority. It is not a full catalogue.
- **Azure SQL Data Discovery & Classification**: column-level labels inside Azure SQL that appear in audit logs.

terms.d: SIT that matches real values from an uploaded, hashed sensitive data table.
ML model that recognises a type of content, such as contracts.
Scanning and metadata service that catalogues and classifies data estate assets.
Defender for Cloud sampling that flags cloud stores holding sensitive data.

lessons.trap: Defender for Cloud sensitive data discovery samples data to prioritise security work. For a complete catalogue with lineage, the answer is Purview Data Map scanning.
lessons.example: A retailer must find every store holding cardholder data across Azure, S3 and on-premises SQL. Purview Data Map scans build the catalogue, and Defender CSPM uses the same SITs to show attack paths to those stores.

lessons.title: Prioritising mitigations for threats to data
lessons.short: Rank data threats by impact and likelihood: ransomware and destruction, exfiltration by external attackers, insider misuse, accidental oversharing, and compliance failure. Protect the most sensitive and business-critical data first. Remove broad access paths, then add encryption, backup immutability, DLP and detection.
lessons.deep:
Budgets are finite, so an architect sets **priorities** for data protection.

1. **Know the data**: discover and classify, then tag business-critical and regulated data.
2. **Map threats** to each data class:
   - **Ransomware and destruction**: immutable backups (Azure Backup **immutable vaults**, **soft delete**, multi-user authorisation) and blob immutability or versioning.
   - **External exfiltration**: remove public network access, use **private endpoints**, disable shared keys and local auth, enforce Entra ID RBAC, and turn on **Defender for Storage/Databases** alerts.
   - **Insider risk**: least privilege, PIM, Purview **DLP**, **Insider Risk Management** and auditing.
   - **Accidental oversharing**: sensitivity labels, sharing controls, access reviews.
   - **Key compromise**: Key Vault RBAC, purge protection, separation of duties.
3. **Prioritise** controls that remove whole attack paths (identity-based access, private networking) over controls that only detect.
4. **Measure** with Defender for Cloud recommendations against the MCSB data protection controls.

Remember that encryption at rest protects against stolen media and platform-level access. It does not stop an attacker who has valid credentials.

terms.d: Unauthorised transfer of data out of the organisation.
Azure Backup vault setting that prevents operations that would delete recovery points early.
Granting only the minimum access needed for the minimum time.
Microsoft cloud security benchmark; its data protection controls guide Azure data security.

lessons.trap: Encryption at rest is a common distractor for credential-based theft. If the attacker has valid access, the data is decrypted for them, so access controls and detection are what matter.
lessons.example: For a health insurer, ransomware against claims data is the top risk. Immutable backups and soft delete come first, then private endpoints and Entra-only access, then DLP on exports.

lessons.title: Encryption at rest, in transit, and Key Vault
lessons.short: Azure encrypts data at rest by default with Microsoft-managed keys (AES-256). Customer-managed keys (CMK) in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM add control. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer at creation. TLS 1.2+ protects data in transit. Managed HSM is single-tenant and FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated.
lessons.deep:
**At rest**: Azure services encrypt data with **256-bit AES**. The key options are:
- **Microsoft-managed keys** (default).
- **Customer-managed keys (CMK)** in **Key Vault** or **Managed HSM**, which you can rotate and revoke. CMK needs **soft delete and purge protection** on the vault.
- **Infrastructure (double) encryption** for Storage adds a second layer with a separate Microsoft-managed key. It must be chosen **when the account is created**.
- **Encryption at host** for VMs covers temp disks and caches. It replaces **Azure Disk Encryption**, which retires on 15 September 2028.

**In transit**: TLS 1.2 or later, HTTPS-only (secure transfer), minimum TLS settings, and IPsec or MACsec for network links.

**In use**: confidential computing (confidential VMs, Always Encrypted secure enclaves).

**Key Vault tiers**: **Standard** (software-protected keys), **Premium** (HSM-backed keys in multitenant HSMs), **Managed HSM** (single-tenant pool you control through its security domain). Premium and Managed HSM firmware is FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated.

**Vault protection**: soft delete is always on (7–90 days, default 90, set at creation, can't be disabled). **Purge protection** is optional, but once enabled it can't be turned off. New vaults default to **Azure RBAC** (API 2026-02-01 and the portal).

terms.d: Key you control in Key Vault or Managed HSM that wraps the service's data encryption key.
Second AES-256 layer for Storage, enabled only at account creation.
Single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSM pool with local RBAC.
Blocks permanent deletion of vaults and objects until the retention period ends.

lessons.trap: Infrastructure encryption can't be added to an existing storage account. The exam expects 'create a new account and migrate'.
lessons.example: A regulator requires keys in single-tenant HSMs that the company alone controls. You choose Managed HSM for SQL TDE and Storage CMK, with purge protection and a rotation policy.

lessons.title: Securing data used in AI workloads
lessons.short: AI workloads add new data paths: training and fine-tuning data, RAG indexes, prompts and responses. Classify the source data, keep document permissions in retrieval, and use managed identities and private endpoints. Add Defender for AI Services for jailbreak and data-leak alerts, Purview DSPM and DLP for AI, and Prompt Shields.
lessons.deep:
With AI, sensitive data can leak through the model, the retrieval layer or the prompts.

**Design controls:**
- **Classify and minimise** training, fine-tuning and grounding data. Don't feed regulated data into a model unless it is needed. Remove secrets.
- **RAG security**: an Azure AI Search index flattens documents, so apply **document-level security filters** (or permission-aware indexing) so users retrieve only what they could open at the source.
- **Identity and network**: apps reach Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI and AI Search with **managed identities** and **Azure RBAC**. Disable key auth where possible, use **private endpoints**, and turn off public access.
- **Encryption**: CMK for Foundry resources and storage holding datasets.
- **Runtime protection**: **Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields** detect jailbreak and indirect prompt injection. **Defender for AI Services** (Defender for Cloud) alerts on jailbreak, data leakage, credential theft and more. It scans text tokens only.
- **Governance**: Microsoft Purview **DSPM** discovers AI apps and interactions. **Endpoint DLP** can block pasting sensitive data into third-party generative AI sites. Insider Risk's **Risky AI usage** template, audit and retention cover prompts and responses.
- **Agents**: give them their own identities (Entra Agent ID) with least privilege.

terms.d: Retrieval-augmented generation: grounding model answers in documents retrieved from an index.
Azure AI Content Safety feature that detects jailbreak and prompt injection attempts.
Defender for Cloud plan with threat detection for Azure OpenAI and Foundry model workloads.
Filtering search results to documents the user is authorised to see.

lessons.trap: A RAG index doesn't inherit SharePoint or file permissions by default. Without security filters, every app user can retrieve every indexed chunk.
lessons.example: An HR chatbot indexes policy and salary documents. Security filters on Entra group IDs, a managed identity to AI Search over private endpoints, and Defender for AI Services stop salary data leaking to all staff.

lessons.title: Data security for Azure SQL and Synapse
lessons.short: Azure SQL layers controls: Microsoft Entra-only authentication, private endpoints, TDE (on by default, optionally with CMK), Always Encrypted for columns hidden from DBAs, dynamic data masking, row-level security, auditing and ledger. Synapse adds managed VNet with data exfiltration protection, which you can only choose at workspace creation.
lessons.deep:
**Azure SQL Database / Managed Instance:**
- **Identity**: **Microsoft Entra-only authentication** turns off SQL logins. Apps use managed identities.
- **Network**: private endpoints, deny public network access, minimum TLS version.
- **TDE**: on by default for new databases with a service-managed key. **TDE with CMK** (Key Vault or Managed HSM) adds key control and revocation.
- **Always Encrypted**: the client driver encrypts columns, so the server and DBAs never see plaintext. Use deterministic encryption for equality lookups and randomised for maximum protection. **Secure enclaves** (VBS; Intel SGX support ends 31 October 2027) allow rich queries and in-place encryption.
- **Dynamic data masking** hides values in query results. It is **not encryption**.
- **Row-level security** filters rows by user.
- **Auditing** to Storage, Log Analytics or Event Hubs. **Ledger** tables (updatable or append-only) give cryptographic **tamper evidence**, with digests stored in immutable storage or Azure Confidential Ledger. A ledger database can't be converted back.

**Azure Synapse Analytics:**
- A **managed virtual network** with **data exfiltration protection** limits outbound traffic to **managed private endpoints** in **approved Entra tenants**. It **can't be enabled after the workspace is created**.
- Dedicated SQL pools support Entra auth, column-level and row-level security, masking and TDE.

terms.d: Client-side column encryption; keys never reach the database engine.
Masks column values in results for non-privileged users; data stays unencrypted.
Azure SQL feature that gives tamper evidence through cryptographic hashes and digests.
Synapse setting that limits egress to managed private endpoints in approved tenants.

lessons.trap: Only Always Encrypted protects data from high-privileged DBAs. TDE is transparent to anyone who can query, and masking is easy to bypass for privileged users.
lessons.example: A payroll database must hide national ID numbers from DBAs while the payroll app still searches by ID. You use Always Encrypted (deterministic) on that column and Entra-only authentication.

lessons.title: Data security for Azure Cosmos DB
lessons.short: Secure Azure Cosmos DB by disabling key-based auth (disableLocalAuth) and using Entra ID with Cosmos DB native data-plane RBAC (Built-in Data Reader/Contributor). Add private endpoints or IP firewall rules, customer-managed keys, client-side Always Encrypted for sensitive properties, and Defender for Azure Cosmos DB.
lessons.deep:
Cosmos DB accounts traditionally use **primary/secondary keys**, which are powerful shared secrets that grant full data access. Modern design:

- **Disable key-based authentication**: set `disableLocalAuth = true` (the portal also offers this at creation). After that, clients must use Microsoft Entra ID.
- **Data-plane RBAC** for the NoSQL API is **native to Cosmos DB**, not Azure RBAC. Role definitions and assignments are stored in the account and managed with `az cosmosdb sql role definition/assignment`. Built-in roles are **Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader** and **Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor**, and you can make custom roles from dataActions.
- **Control-plane** access uses normal Azure RBAC (for example **Cosmos DB Operator**). `disableKeyBasedMetadataWriteAccess` stops key holders changing databases and containers.
- **Network**: private endpoints, disable public network access, or IP/VNet firewall rules.
- **Encryption**: always encrypted at rest. Add a **CMK** in Key Vault. **Always Encrypted for Cosmos DB** encrypts chosen properties on the client.
- **Threat detection**: **Defender for Azure Cosmos DB** (part of the Defender for Databases plans) alerts on SQL injection patterns, anomalous access and suspicious key extraction.
- Continuous backup with point-in-time restore helps recovery.

terms.d: Cosmos DB account property that blocks primary/secondary key authentication.
Native role system for data access, separate from Azure RBAC.
Native role allowing read and write of items and containers.
Threat protection for Cosmos DB within Defender for Cloud.

lessons.trap: Assigning an Azure RBAC role such as Cosmos DB Operator doesn't grant data access. Data-plane roles are Cosmos DB native assignments.
lessons.example: An order service's account keys leaked in a log file. You rotate the keys, set disableLocalAuth, grant the app's managed identity Built-in Data Contributor, and enable Defender for Azure Cosmos DB.

lessons.title: Data security for Azure Storage
lessons.short: Secure Azure Storage with Entra ID RBAC instead of account keys (disallow Shared Key), user delegation SAS, private endpoints and firewall rules, no anonymous blob access, and secure transfer. Use CMK and infrastructure encryption where required. Protect against deletion with soft delete, versioning and immutable (WORM) policies.
lessons.deep:
Storage accounts are a favourite target because one leaked key exposes everything.

**Access:**
- Use **Entra ID** with data roles (Storage Blob Data Reader, Contributor and others) and managed identities.
- **Disallow Shared Key** (`--allow-shared-key-access false`, Azure Policy *Storage accounts should prevent shared key access*). This blocks account keys, **account SAS and service SAS**. **User delegation SAS**, which is signed with Entra credentials, still works.
- Disable anonymous blob access. Set SAS expiration policies.

**Network**: private endpoints, deny public network access or restrict with firewall rules, and **secure transfer required** with a minimum TLS version.

**Encryption**: AES-256 by default. Add **CMK** (Key Vault needs soft delete and purge protection, RSA 2048/3072/4096 keys) and, if mandated, **infrastructure encryption** (at creation only).

**Data protection against ransomware and errors**:
- **Soft delete** for blobs and containers, plus **versioning** and point-in-time restore.
- **Immutable storage (WORM)**: **time-based retention** (1 to 146,000 days) or **legal hold**. A **locked** time-based policy can't be shortened or deleted, which is needed for SEC 17a-4(f). Unlocked is for testing only.
- A resource lock to prevent account deletion.

terms.d: Account key authorisation; disallowing it also disables account and service SAS.
SAS signed with Entra credentials; works when Shared Key is disallowed.
WORM policy; once locked it can only be extended.
WORM hold with no fixed end date that stays until it is cleared.

lessons.trap: An unlocked immutability policy can still be shortened or deleted, so it doesn't meet regulatory WORM requirements. The policy must be locked.
lessons.example: A broker must keep trade records for seven years, unchangeable even by admins. You apply a locked time-based retention policy of 2,557 days and disallow Shared Key.

lessons.title: Defender for Storage and Defender for Databases
lessons.short: Defender for Storage detects threats in Blob, Files and Data Lake: activity monitoring, malware scanning on upload or on demand, and sensitive data threat detection. Defender for Databases covers Azure SQL, SQL servers on machines, open-source relational databases and Cosmos DB, with threat alerts and vulnerability assessment.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft Defender for Storage** (Defender for Cloud):
- **Activity monitoring**: ML and threat intelligence analyse control- and data-plane telemetry, such as access from Tor or unusual data extraction. It **doesn't need resource logs** and doesn't affect performance.
- **Malware scanning**: Microsoft Defender Antivirus scans blobs **on upload** or **on demand** (up to 50 GB per blob). It is billed per GB scanned, with a default cap of 10,000 GB per account per month. Results go to **blob index tags** (not tamper-resistant), Defender alerts, optional **Event Grid** events and the Log Analytics `StorageMalwareScanningResults` table. Built-in **automated remediation can soft-delete malicious blobs**.
- **Sensitive data threat detection**: no extra cost. It uses Purview SITs to raise the severity of alerts on sensitive stores.
- Priced per storage account. Enable at **subscription level** (with exclusions) and enforce with Azure Policy.

**Microsoft Defender for Databases** is four plans:
- **Defender for Azure SQL Databases** and **Defender for SQL Servers on Machines** (Azure, on-premises or multicloud through Azure Arc): **vulnerability assessment** plus **advanced threat protection** (SQL injection, brute force, anomalous access).
- **Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases** (Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL).
- **Defender for Azure Cosmos DB**.

Alerts flow into Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel.

terms.d: Defender for Storage antivirus scan of blobs on upload or on demand.
Behavioural threat detection on storage operations without enabling logs.
Defender for SQL scan for database misconfigurations and excessive permissions.
Group of Defender for Cloud plans for SQL, open-source relational and Cosmos DB.

lessons.trap: Malware scanning blob index tags can be changed by anyone with write access, so don't use them as the only gate. Use alerts, Event Grid or automated remediation.
lessons.example: A claims portal accepts customer uploads. On-upload malware scanning with automated soft-delete remediation and an Event Grid-triggered function moves clean files to processing.

questions.stem: Which metric defines the maximum amount of data, measured in time, that a business can afford to lose after an incident?
options: Recovery time objective (RTO)
Recovery point objective (RPO)
Mean time to detect (MTTD)
Service level agreement (SLA)
questions.explain: RPO measures tolerable data loss (for example, last 15 minutes). RTO is how long the service may be down. MTTD measures detection speed, and an SLA is a contracted availability commitment, not a data-loss target.

questions.stem: You need the Microsoft Defender portal to automatically flag domain controllers and accounts holding the Privileged Role Administrator role as crown jewels, so attack paths and incidents involving them are prioritised. What should you use?
options: Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard
Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk policies
Microsoft Security Exposure Management critical asset management
Microsoft Purview Data Map classifications
questions.explain: Critical asset management in Exposure Management ships predefined classifications (domain controllers, privileged roles, sensitive databases, cloud resources) and surfaces criticality in attack paths and incidents. ID Protection scores identity risk, the compliance dashboard tracks standards, and Purview Data Map classifies data, not assets.

questions.case: Fabrikam's CISO has a limited budget for next year. A risk workshop showed that an outage of the order-to-cash process costs $2M per day, while most internal tools could be offline for a week without material loss. The board asks for a resiliency strategy that reduces business impact from attacks as quickly as possible.
questions.stem: What should the architect do first?
options: Deploy the same controls to every system to avoid gaps
Run an organisation-wide phishing simulation to measure user awareness
Purchase a SIEM so all logs are centralised before any other work
Map order-to-cash to its supporting IT assets and set RTO/RPO targets for them
questions.explain: Resiliency strategy starts from business impact: identify the critical process's assets (apps, data, identity, backups) and set recovery targets, then prioritise controls. Uniform controls waste limited budget; a SIEM or phishing test may help later but don't prioritise the critical assets.

questions.stem: For each statement about a resiliency strategy, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Identity systems such as Microsoft Entra ID and AD DS should be treated as business-critical assets.
Under the assume breach principle, the strategy can focus only on preventing initial access.
A lower RTO generally requires more investment, such as replication instead of restore-from-backup only.

questions.explain: Identity controls everything, so it is critical. Assume breach requires planning detection, containment and recovery, not just prevention. Lower RTO usually means costlier designs like Site Recovery replication.

questions.stem: By default, how long does Azure Backup keep soft-deleted backup data recoverable at no extra cost?
options: 7 days
14 days
30 days
180 days
questions.explain: Soft delete defaults to 14 days, with no cost within that window. It can be configured from 14 up to 180 days, with extra days billed. 7 and 30 days are not the default.

questions.stem: You must ensure no one, including a compromised Global Administrator, can ever turn off the protection that stops recovery points in a Recovery Services vault being deleted early. Which configuration meets the requirement?
options: Enable soft delete with 180-day retention
Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock to the vault
Enable immutability on the vault and lock it
Enable immutability on the vault without locking it
questions.explain: Only an immutable vault in the 'Enabled and locked' state is irreversible. Unlocked immutability can be disabled. A resource lock can be removed by an owner, and soft delete protects deleted data but doesn't stop someone reducing retention.

questions.case: Tailspin's backup administrators hold Backup Contributor on all Recovery Services vaults. A red team showed that a stolen backup admin account could disable security features and then delete backups. Tailspin wants a second person to approve critical vault operations, with the strongest isolation possible.
questions.stem: Which design should you recommend?
options: Enable MUA with a Resource Guard in the same subscription, and give backup admins Contributor on it
Enable MUA with a Resource Guard in a separate security tenant; grant Backup MUA Operator just in time
Require a backup security PIN for all operations and store it in Key Vault
Assign backup admins the Backup Operator role instead of Backup Contributor
questions.explain: A Resource Guard in a different tenant gives maximum isolation; the security admin grants Backup MUA Operator temporarily (for example via PIM). Giving backup admins Contributor on the guard defeats MUA. A PIN or role downgrade doesn't add a second approver.

questions.stem: Which TWO operations are mandatory protected operations (cannot be excluded) when a vault is associated with a Resource Guard for multi-user authorization? Select TWO.
options: Disable soft delete or security features
Restore a backup item
Remove MUA protection
Modify a backup policy
Get backup security PIN
questions.explain: Disabling soft delete/security features and removing MUA protection are mandatory. Modify policy and get security PIN are optional (enabled by default), and Restore is optional and disabled by default.

questions.stem: For each statement about Azure Backup immutable vaults, select Yes if true.

statements.s: An immutable vault blocks reducing the retention in a backup policy.
An immutable vault blocks increasing the retention in a backup policy.
Immutable vault is available for both Recovery Services vaults and Backup vaults.

questions.explain: Immutability prevents actions that could lose recovery points, such as reducing retention; increasing retention is allowed. Both vault types support immutability (time-based immutability is Recovery Services vault only).

questions.stem: Which Azure service replicates on-premises VMware VMs to Azure and orchestrates failover using recovery plans?
options: Azure Backup with the MARS agent
Azure Migrate
Azure Site Recovery
Azure Business Continuity Center
questions.explain: Azure Site Recovery replicates VMware, Hyper-V and physical machines to Azure and sequences failover with recovery plans. MARS backs up files/folders; Azure Migrate is for one-time migration; Business Continuity Center is a management view, not a replication engine.

questions.stem: An architect proposes Azure Site Recovery as the only protection against ransomware for a file server, arguing it gives a 5-minute RTO. What is the main flaw?
options: Site Recovery cannot replicate Windows file servers
Site Recovery has no support for test failover
Site Recovery replicates only between Azure regions, not from on-premises
Encrypted data replicates to the target, so point-in-time immutable backups are still needed
questions.explain: Replication faithfully copies corruption and encryption, so ransomware recovery needs point-in-time backups that attackers can't alter. Site Recovery supports Windows servers, on-premises sources, and non-disruptive test failover, so the other options are false.

questions.case: Northwind runs SQL Server and Hyper-V VMs in two on-premises datacentres and is moving some workloads to Azure. Requirements: back up on-premises SQL Server and Hyper-V workloads to Azure; back up selected file shares on branch servers with no local backup server; prove recovery works every quarter without impacting production.
questions.stem: Which THREE components should you include? Select THREE.
options: Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS)
MARS agent on the branch servers
Site Recovery test failovers and scheduled restore drills
Azure Migrate replication appliance
Azure Files sync to replace backups
questions.explain: MABS protects on-premises workloads such as SQL Server and Hyper-V; the MARS agent backs up files and folders directly to Azure without a backup server; test failovers and restore drills validate recovery non-disruptively. Azure Migrate is for migration, and file sync isn't a backup.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to design a BCDR solution for a critical workload.
options: Identify the business process and its dependent IT assets
Agree RTO and RPO targets with the business owner
Select backup and replication services that meet the targets
Protect backups with isolation, immutability and MUA
Run test failovers and restore drills and measure recovery time
questions.explain: BCDR design flows from business impact to targets, then technology choice, then hardening the recovery copies, then validating that recovery actually meets the targets.

questions.stem: Put Microsoft's ransomware protection steps in priority order.
options: Prepare your ransomware recovery plan
Limit the scope of ransomware damage
Make it hard for cybercriminals to get in
questions.explain: Microsoft prioritises recovery readiness (remove the reason to pay), then protecting privileged roles (limit blast radius), then hardening entry points, which takes longest and must not delay the first two.

questions.stem: You plan to deploy Defender for Endpoint attack surface reduction (ASR) rules to block Office macros from launching child processes across 20,000 devices. What should you do first?
options: Enable the rules in block mode for all devices immediately
Enable the rules in audit mode and assess the impact
Disable tamper protection so the rules can be applied
Deploy the rules only to domain controllers
questions.explain: Microsoft's guidance is to run ASR rules in audit mode first, review the impact on business apps, then switch to block. Immediate block risks outages; disabling tamper protection weakens defences; ASR rules targeting Office belong on user endpoints.

questions.case: Adatum suffered a human-operated ransomware attack. Attackers stole data, then encrypted file servers. Backups existed but were on a domain-joined server and were deleted using a compromised domain admin account. Restore procedures were stored on the encrypted file share.
questions.stem: Which recommendation BEST addresses the root causes of the failed recovery?
options: Add more email filtering rules in Defender for Office 365
Replace the file servers with Azure Files
Increase the number of domain admin accounts so recovery can proceed if one is locked
Keep backups in immutable, separately administered storage and protect recovery documents off-site
questions.explain: Recovery failed because backups were reachable by the compromised identity and procedures were encrypted. Immutable, isolated backups and protected recovery documentation fix that. Email filtering addresses entry, not recovery; more domain admins increases risk; Azure Files alone doesn't protect backups.

questions.stem: For each statement about human-operated ransomware, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Attackers commonly steal credentials and move laterally before deploying ransomware.
Paying the ransom guarantees that a working decryption key will be provided.
Attackers often exfiltrate data before encryption to add extortion pressure.

questions.explain: Human-operated attacks rely on credential theft and lateral movement and often steal data for extortion. Payment never guarantees recovery, which is why Microsoft prioritises recovery readiness.

questions.stem: In the enterprise access model, which plane contains Microsoft Entra ID and AD DS domain controllers?
options: Management plane
Data/workload plane
User access
Control plane
questions.explain: The control plane holds centralised identity and access control systems, expanding the legacy Tier 0. The management plane covers enterprise IT management, the data/workload plane holds business apps and data, and user access covers user pathways.

questions.stem: Incident analysis shows attackers moved from one compromised workstation to 300 others using the same local Administrator password. Which control BEST prevents this lateral traversal?
options: Windows LAPS
Microsoft Entra Password Protection
BitLocker Drive Encryption
Defender SmartScreen
questions.explain: Windows LAPS gives every device a unique, rotated local admin password, so one stolen password doesn't unlock others. Password Protection blocks weak passwords for accounts, BitLocker protects data at rest, and SmartScreen warns about malicious sites and files.

questions.case: Litware has 25 users with permanent Global Administrator. Admins read email and browse the web from the same laptops they use for the Entra admin center. Leadership wants to reduce ransomware blast radius within 90 days without blocking emergency access.
questions.stem: Which THREE actions should you recommend? Select THREE.
options: Convert permanent Global Administrator assignments to PIM eligible assignments with approval
Require privileged access workstations for administrative sessions, enforced with Conditional Access
Keep two monitored emergency access accounts with phishing-resistant credentials
Grant all admins Global Administrator permanently so incidents can be handled faster
Disable MFA for admins on trusted networks to reduce friction
questions.explain: PIM removes standing privilege, PAWs enforced by Conditional Access separate admin work from risky activity, and monitored break-glass accounts preserve emergency access. Permanent Global Admin and disabling MFA increase blast radius.

questions.stem: You need one native Azure solution to assess and install OS updates for Azure VMs and for Linux servers running in AWS, using maintenance windows and no Log Analytics dependency. What should you recommend?
options: Windows Autopatch
Azure Update Manager with the AWS servers onboarded to Azure Arc
Azure Automation Update Management
Microsoft Intune update rings
questions.explain: Azure Update Manager manages Windows and Linux servers in Azure and, via Azure Arc, in other clouds and on-premises, with maintenance windows and no Log Analytics dependency. Autopatch and Intune update rings target client devices; Automation Update Management depended on Log Analytics and has been superseded.

questions.stem: Complete the Azure Resource Graph query that lists the latest patch assessment results for virtual machines.
questions.code:
____
| where type =~ "microsoft.compute/virtualmachines/patchassessmentresults"
| project id, properties.status, properties.lastModifiedDateTime
options: securityresources
patchassessmentresources
advisorresources
policyresources
questions.explain: Azure Update Manager writes assessment results to the patchassessmentresources table in Resource Graph. securityresources holds Defender for Cloud data, advisorresources holds Advisor recommendations, and policyresources holds Azure Policy states.

questions.stem: Which Microsoft resource provides diagrams that map Microsoft security capabilities across a hybrid, multicloud estate, including attack chain coverage and security operations views?
options: Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architectures (MCRA)
Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)
Azure Well-Architected Framework (WAF)
Microsoft Compliance Manager
questions.explain: MCRA is a set of reference architecture diagrams showing how Microsoft capabilities fit together, including attack chain coverage and SecOps. MCSB is a control set, WAF guides workload design, and Compliance Manager tracks regulatory assessments.

questions.stem: A security architect wants to compare the company's existing third-party tools against Microsoft's recommended end-to-end capabilities and identify integration points and gaps. Which resource should be the starting template?
options: Azure landing zone accelerator
Microsoft Secure Score
Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architectures (MCRA)
Microsoft cloud security benchmark compliance dashboard
questions.explain: MCRA is designed as a target-state template and comparison reference to find gaps and integration points with existing tools. The landing zone accelerator deploys Azure foundations, Secure Score measures Microsoft-configured posture, and the compliance dashboard tracks control status.

questions.stem: For each statement about the MCRA, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The MCRA includes guidance on operational technology (OT) and multicloud environments.
The MCRA defines prescriptive control IDs such as NS-1 that Defender for Cloud assesses.
The MCRA is aligned with Zero Trust principles.

questions.explain: MCRA covers the 'hybrid of everything' including OT and multicloud, built on Zero Trust. Control IDs like NS-1 come from the MCSB, which Defender for Cloud assesses.

questions.stem: Which security standard is assigned by default when you enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud on an Azure subscription?
options: CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
Microsoft cloud security benchmark
questions.explain: MCSB is the default standard in Defender for Cloud for Azure, AWS and GCP, and drives Secure Score. CIS, NIST and ISO standards can be added through the regulatory compliance settings but aren't assigned by default.

questions.stem: In the MCSB, which control domain covers requirements such as protecting Recovery Services vaults and validating restores?
options: BR (Backup and recovery)
DP (Data protection)
IR (Incident response)
PV (Posture and vulnerability management)
questions.explain: Backup and recovery (BR) covers backup coverage, protecting backups and validating recovery. DP focuses on data classification and encryption, IR on incident handling, and PV on configuration and vulnerability management.

questions.stem: A company runs workloads in Azure, AWS and GCP and wants a single security baseline with posture recommendations across all three. Which TWO statements are correct? Select TWO.
options: Defender for Cloud assesses connected AWS and GCP environments against MCSB by default
MCSB applies only to Azure, so the company must use the CIS benchmarks for AWS and GCP
MCSB control mappings to frameworks such as NIST prove the company is fully compliant
MCSB recommendations contribute to Defender for Cloud Secure Score
MCSB can only be assessed by third-party CSPM tools
